RAVENS' RASHOD BATEMAN FACES DOMESTIC CHARGES FOR ALLEGED ATTACK ON CAR CARRYING EX-GIRLFRIEND AND THEIR BABY

Stepping to the podium Thursday, Weaver backed Humphrey's benching.

Marlon Humphrey No. 44 of the Baltimore Ravens warms up on the field before a game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on Nov. 1, 2026, in Orchard Park, N.Y. (Getty Images)

"This is a learning moment," Weaver said. "In this day and age, I think it's important for these guys to understand that, yes, you have freedom of speech. You can say what it is you want to say, on your phone, on your platform, whatever that is. But that doesn't give you freedom of consequence."

RAVENS PLAYERS RIDE WITH PRESIDENT TRUMP IN MOTORCADE, GET SHOUTOUT DURING SPEECH AT BALTIMORE SHIPYARD EVENT

"I think that's where we're at," Weaver added. "So, we're living in that, regardless of intent. He said the things that he said, which obviously is negative toward where we live and where we love."

Even while endorsing the benching, Weaver distinguished between Humphrey's character and his poor judgment.

MARLON HUMPHREY SAYS MEETING PRESIDENT TRUMP INSPIRED HIM TO VOTE IN THE NEXT ELECTION

"I think as a dad, as a coach, as a Christian, it's important to say that I can love the man, have respect for him, and disagree with what he said in this particular moment," Weaver said.

Running a podcast is easier when you are actually playing well, and Humphrey hasn't been.

"I think it's safe to say that, defensively, we haven't lived up to our standard," Weaver admitted. "So, as it pertains to him individually, I think a lot of his errors have been a product of technique and fundamentals."

Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on before the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on Nov. 5, 2026, in Baltimore, Md. (Getty Images)

"That's weird to say for a guy that's been at his stature for such a long time, but it's one of those things where you're constantly sharpening and making sure your tires are aligned as a player."

"It's very easy to get comfortable and start to let those things go by the wayside a little bit," Weaver said. "When that happens, you give up plays like that. Particularly as you age, you're just not able to rely on your pure athleticism, maybe as you once did."

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
excerpt:
Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major AI data centre project in Canada that has so far been embraced by legislators.

As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence...
body_text:
Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major AI data centre project in Canada that has so far been embraced by legislators.

As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.

While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.

"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.

At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".

One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.

His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.

Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign., external The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75%, external, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.

Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.

The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.

The project is billed as "off-grid", external, relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment, external, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.

The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June , externalthat he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".

In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.

Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.

"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.

Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.

He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.

Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.

"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press, external, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.

This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.

There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.

On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre, external that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.

But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.

"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.

"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.

BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the US

So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.

The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.

Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.

Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.

"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.

Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.

If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.

MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta,, external over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.

But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.

"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."

'We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'

Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?

Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff

title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
excerpt:
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has on...
body_text:
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis

Who are the Houthis and what do they want?

title: Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
excerpt:
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.

Boubacar Se...
body_text:
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.

Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.

A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.

The number of people still missing remains unclear.

The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.

New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.

The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.

The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).

Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.

Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.

The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.

As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.

But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.

“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.

“We need to fix the root causes of this problem.”

title: Trump clears hurdle in $15 billion lawsuit against New York Times
excerpt:
President Donald Trump’s legal team is celebrating Thursday after a judge denied The New York Times’ motion to dismiss the president’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit. (Getty Images/iStock)

President ...
body_text:
President Donald Trump’s legal team is celebrating Thursday after a judge denied The New York Times’ motion to dismiss the president’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit. (Getty Images/iStock)

President Donald Trump’s legal team is celebrating Thursday after a judge denied The New York Times’ motion to dismiss the president’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the paper.

U.S. District Judge Steven D. Merryday allowed four counts centered on seven specific accusations of criminal conduct to move forward after Trump’s legal team argued that the Times and publisher Penguin Random House showed reckless disregard, alleging "purposeful avoidance of the truth" in a book authored by Times journalists.

"President Trump continues holding the Fake News accountable for deceiving the American people. Judge Merryday has correctly denied the motion to dismiss filed by The New York Times, Penguin Publishing and their writers as to President Trump’s powerhouse defamation lawsuit," a spokesman for Trump’s legal team told Fox News Digital.

NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER

A spokesman for Trump’s legal team told Fox News Digital, "President Trump continues holding the Fake News accountable for deceiving the American people." (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"These defendants will now have to answer for intentionally and maliciously defaming President Trump," the spokesman continued. "The New York Times has a long pattern of defaming President Trump in service of its leftist political agenda, and today’s momentous ruling is a victory for honesty in America."

Judge Merryday issued a pointed critique of Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner, the authors of "Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success," for publishing definitive claims of complex tax fraud and money laundering without a formal legal opinion or forensic auditing.

Merryday observed that accusations were made against Trump and his father without charges or convictions.

"In other words, the facts alleged in the complaint create at least a plausible inference that the authors and the publishers knew that no reliable conclusion about violations of the tax laws, including especially the estate and gift tax laws, is possible without reliance on qualified opinion formulated after the necessary factual and legal research and analysis, which they knowingly failed to obtain," Merryday wrote.

TRUMP TOUTS LEGAL VICTORY OVER BBC AS JUDGE SAYS HIS LAWSUIT AGAINST BRITISH BROADCASTER CAN PROCEED

President Donald Trump’s legal team argued The New York Times and Penguin Publishing showed reckless disregard. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)

The court dismissed the Times’ reliance on outside commentators, such as a former prosecutor saying a Trump transaction "smells like a crime" and a professor who called the action "suspicious."

"Obviously, even a qualified expert offering a superficial characterization such as a transaction is ‘suspicious’ or ‘could’ violate the law or attributing to a transaction the ‘smell’ of crime or noting that a gift tax return can evade IRS scrutiny or generously giving his immensely valuable time to aid laypersons ‘lost in the weeds’ is far from a formal legal opinion sufficient to remove serious doubt about the truthfulness and accuracy of a statement accusing a specific person of fraud or tax evasion or some related crime arising from a specific transaction," Merryday wrote.

While Trump’s lawsuit can move forward, Merryday also dismissed two counts and threw out 27 other challenged statements as non-actionable under the strict First Amendment protections of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan and denied Trump's request to amend his complaint a third time.

TRUMP DOJ WITHDRAWS SUBPOENAS TARGETING NEW YORK TIMES JOURNALISTS AMID LEAK PROBE

The New York Times told Fox News Digital the lawsuit has "no legal merit."  (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

A New York Times spokesperson provided the following statement to Fox News Digital: "The Times is encouraged to see Judge Merryday’s dismissal of almost all claims against us. We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country."

The judge ordered The New York Times to file a formal answer within 28 days.

Fox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.

title: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
excerpt:
Rose was a 17-time Major League Baseball All-Star, but his legacy was tarnished by a lifetime ban

US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a ...
body_text:
Rose was a 17-time Major League Baseball All-Star, but his legacy was tarnished by a lifetime ban

US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball   (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.

The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.

According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".

The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.

Because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.

The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.

The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.

"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.

MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.

In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.

In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

Major League Baseball legend Rose dies aged 83

title: Ukraine plans to double drone supplies, triple deep strikes
excerpt: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine plans to double its drone supplies and more than triple its long-range strike capabilities next year, according to Ukraine’s defense minister, as Kyiv presses ahead with its lo...
body_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine plans to double its drone supplies and more than triple its long-range strike capabilities next year, according to Ukraine’s defense minister, as Kyiv presses ahead with its long-range strike campaign despite the Pentagon’s criticism of attacks deep inside Russia.

Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara made the announcements Tuesday at a press conference after the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels.

“There are prospects in this, and we are only getting started,” he said.

A day later, the British government said in a statement that it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly more than 620 miles (1,000 kilometers), in a roughly $342 million (£260 million) package.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce the offer Thursday in Berlin at a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” of Ukraine supporters, where U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steven Witkoff are expected to brief European leaders on peace negotiations.

Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.

Khmara told the EU Foreign Affairs Council that drones will make up more than half of Ukraine’s weapons needs in 2027. At the press conference, he said 62% of funding should go to drones, including first-person-view, middle-strike, deep-strike and logistics drones.

“While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line,” Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said in his opening remarks to the meeting.

Such strikes, “especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate,” he said.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius responded in a press conference after the meeting, stating that faulting strikes on “strategic military and military use targets” in Russia is “quite a stupid thing, I think.”

“We should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heater infrastructure in Ukraine,” Pistorius said.

Colby left the meeting shortly after his own remarks, before the press conference, according to two sources cited by The Telegraph, one of whom said he did not stay for Khmara’s classified briefing.

Colby “definitely appeared more on the side of Russia than on the side of Ukraine,” a German source told the publication.

Colby’s remarks follow pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv to spare Russian refineries.

Colby also said that strikes that target “Russia’s warmaking machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advance on the front lines” and that Ukraine should not “be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back.”

Further support from European allies announced at the meeting included a pledge by Germany to buy jointly produced middle-strike and deep-strike drones, and a promise from Norway to set aside $300 million to buy Ukrainian drones, according to a Defense Ministry readout.

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said at the same press conference that deep strikes have “helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives.” He also said Colby’s attendance in person was “a further demonstration of U.S. commitment and involvement.”

Britain’s new drones will let Ukraine target “military production facilities and other legitimate military targets far behind the front lines,” according to a government statement.

“It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” Britain’s Streeting said.

Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia’s full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.

title: France and Sweden hold first joint nuclear-deterrence exercise
excerpt: PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A3...
body_text:
PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A330 MRTT tanker aircraft operating over Sweden alongside Swedish Gripen fighters.

The exercise, dubbed Excalibur, was held in northern Sweden on Nov. 16 to 18, with the aim of improving interoperability between the French and Swedish air forces, the two countries’ armed forces said in statements on Thursday. The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.

The French-Swedish cooperation follows an exercise last month in which British Eurofighter Typhoon jets escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission. France has been working with several European allies to implement Macron’s proposal to bolster European deterrence, in the face of nuclear saber-rattling by Russia and uncertainty about United States security guarantees.

France’s nuclear deterrent consists of an ocean-based component comprising strategic ballistic-missile submarines, as well as an airborne component consisting of Rafale jets capable of carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles developed by MBDA.

“Since the in-depth dialogue on ‘forward deterrence’ was initiated, France and Sweden are taking steps to implement their common roadmap for strategic cooperation,” the Swedish Armed Forces said. The exercise “demonstrates our joint readiness and capability to act together and reflects the commitment of our two countries towards deterring threats and strengthening allied security.”

The deployment of the Rafale jets alongside Gripen fighters, with the support of an A330 MRTT, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the two air forces in the areas of nuclear deterrence, in the service of Europe’s security, the French Armed Forces General Staff said in a post on the social network X.

“This type of deployment not only allows to test the dispersion of French aircraft to improve their capability to survive an adversary disabling strike, but also opens the door for new modes of operation previously unimaginable, such as attacking targets deep within the Russian Arctic or planning much smaller raids without needing in-flight refueling,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X.

Sweden’s Gripen fighters are “excellent combat aircraft” specifically designed to penetrate Russian ground-to-air and air-to-air defense systems, and they could be valuable assets during a nuclear strike mission, while freeing up conventional Rafale jets for other missions, Marcuz said.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

title: South Korean court orders retrial for ex-PM Han over martial law attempt
excerpt: South Korea’s Supreme Court has ⁠⁠overturned the 15-year prison sentence of former Prime ⁠⁠Minister Han Duck-soo for his role in the brief imposition of martial law two years ago, sending the case bac...
body_text:
South Korea’s Supreme Court has ⁠⁠overturned the 15-year prison sentence of former Prime ⁠⁠Minister Han Duck-soo for his role in the brief imposition of martial law two years ago, sending the case back ⁠⁠to a lower court.

A majority of justices found shortcomings in the lower court’s assessment of Han’s actions before former President Yoon Suk Yeol’s declaration, particularly his proposal to convene a Cabinet meeting that could have given legitimacy to the president’s decision.

The justices said it was difficult to establish whether Han had intended to undermine the Constitution, given the urgent circumstances at the time.

The special prosecution team for Han’s case said in a statement that they respect the ⁠⁠court’s ruling.

The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation.

In the aftermath of the imposition of martial law, former President Yoon was impeached and removed from office by the Constitutional Court in April 2025.

A presidential election two months later brought Lee Jae Myung to power.

Yoon’s 2024 decree plunged the country into chaos, but lasted only about six hours as opposition lawmakers scrambled to overturn the decision.

Han, 77, one of several top officials sentenced over the short-lived martial law bid, was handed a 23-year jail term in January for his involvement, which the court said threatened “the constitutional order” and amounted to insurrection.

An appeals court then reduced the sentence to 15 years in May, citing Han’s “more than 50 years as a public official prior to the martial law declaration”.

Han has denied wrongdoing in relation to ⁠⁠all charges except one for perjury. He said last year that while he regretted not being able to stop Yoon from declaring martial law, he “never agreed to it or tried to help”.

Yoon, meanwhile, has ⁠⁠denied wrongdoing and said he exercised his powers as president. He was convicted of insurrection in February and sentenced to life in ⁠⁠prison.

He has appealed and awaits that ruling, which ⁠⁠is scheduled for January.

title: Homeowner says squatter hijacked his property in affluent community, stole deed in $1 scheme
excerpt:
Washington homeowner Ellis Cameron spoke with Fox News Digital about how a property manager allegedly took over his rental home in an affluent community, sparking a months-long squatter battle.

A hom...
body_text:
Washington homeowner Ellis Cameron spoke with Fox News Digital about how a property manager allegedly took over his rental home in an affluent community, sparking a months-long squatter battle.

A homeowner’s lucrative rental property investment within an affluent Pacific Northwest community was allegedly hijacked by the very property manager he hired, sparking a months-long squatter standoff that ended with a $1 deed, a shooting on the property and the manager behind bars.

Ellis Cameron shared his story with Fox News Digital and says he hired Junior Patrick Adelbai to manage property he purchased and renovated in Edgewood, Washington. Instead of managing the rental, the homeowner said the alleged squatter decided to move his family in, causing a months-long legal battle for the homeowner and making him unable to sell it.

The homeowner intended to have Adelbai rent out the property for $6,500 a month. After the pair reached an agreement, Cameron changed the locks to prep it for renters.

A before and after photo shows how an alleged squatter trashed a homeowner's property, he said. (Ellis Cameron)

SQUATTER NIGHTMARE TURNS DC APARTMENT BUILDING INTO 'DRUG HAVEN' AS LEGAL BATTLE DRAGS ON: 'THERE'S NO HELP'

"The very next day, he broke the locks, went into the house, and brought his wife and his two kids, and instead of doing [things] according to our agreement, he decided that he would just squat there, live there for free."

The homeowner said Adelbai moved his family in and lived in the house without running water for nearly two months – and made a mess of the inside and outside of the property, as depicted in a series of photos he shared with Fox News Digital.

Edgewood is located near Tacoma, Washington, pictured here with Mount Rainier in the distance on Commencement Bay. (Getty Images)

NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'

Cameron said he was left paying the mortgage without the rental income he was anticipating to cover the payments.

Ellis Cameron says property manager Junior Patrick Adelbai broke the locks on his rental home and moved his wife and two children inside without permission. (Ellis Cameron)

He asked the family to leave on numerous occasions, enlisting the help of law enforcement at times, but was told the dispute was a "civil matter" that would have to be resolved through the court system.

'TOXIC COCKTAIL' OF RENTER PROTECTIONS DESTROYED $39M AFFORDABLE HOUSING INVESTMENT AS DEM CITIES FOLLOW SUIT

"You have squatter-friendly laws that protect the squatters," Cameron said. "In Washington state, especially Pierce County, it's a high-risk agreement to decide to rent your place out because if something doesn't go right, it's going to be problematic for you. In Washington state, you can't turn off the squatters' utilities, you can't threaten them."

ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS

State law says landlords cannot evict tenants on their own. Instead, they must notify law enforcement, give proper notice and let courts handle the removal.

Junior Patrick Adelbai allegedly filed a quitclaim deed transferring ownership of a Washington rental property to his wife for just $1. (Ellis Cameron)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Making matters worse, the homeowner said Adelbai's wife weaponized law enforcement against him when he tried to show the home in hopes of selling it.

"She held my place sabotaged for months because the law protected her," he said.

HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY

Cameron went on to say, "I had a real estate agent [give] a 48-hour notice to the squatter, and she called the police when [the agent] showed up and [she told police] she didn't want to show the place."

A Washington homeowner says an alleged squatter lived in his rental property without running water for nearly two months. (Ellis Cameron)

The situation reached a breaking point when Adelbai allegedly shot at someone on the property in March, claiming self-defense while simultaneously claiming he was the homeowner, Cameron said.

HIS HOME CHANGED HANDS FOR $5. COULD IT HAPPEN TO YOUR FAMILY?

The situation escalated March 19, when records show a quitclaim deed prepared and signed by Adelbai was filed with the Pierce County Auditor’s Office, KIRO7 reported.

Adelbai claimed he owned the property in the document and transferred ownership to his wife, Karmaleen Issac, for $1.

ARIZONA MAN SAYS HE LOST $475K HOME TO HOA FORECLOSURE OVER LESS THAN $1,000 IN UNPAID DUES

Ellis Cameron says his rental property was left in disrepair after the alleged squatter's arrest and that he remains unable to sell the home. (Ellis Cameron)

When asked how a fraudulent deed could be approved, the Pierce County Auditor’s Office told Fox News Digital that their hands are tied by state law, which dictates that they cannot legally refuse to record a document—or assess its legality—as long as it meets basic formatting criteria.

"Title fraud is devastating, and the law needs to change. More protection is needed in Washington state and nationwide," Pierce County Auditor Linda Farmer said.

FLORIDA REAL ESTATE SEES SURGE FROM WASHINGTON HIGH EARNERS FLEEING NEW MILLIONAIRE INCOME TAX

The auditor's office noted they are currently co-chairing a statewide workgroup tracking national models to propose new measures to the Washington State Legislature. In the interim, Pierce County has launched a free "Owner Alert" service, which notifies homeowners of suspicious filings so they can take rapid legal action. Over 7,000 residents have already signed up.

Ellis Cameron says he continued paying the mortgage on his investment property despite receiving no rental income during the months-long squatter dispute. (Ellis Cameron)

Meanwhile, Adelbai is currently in jail with a list of pending charges. The Pierce County Sheriff's Office confirmed the suspect's arrest to Fox News Digital, but did not provide details into the incident or shooting.

Cameron said following the arrest, the family moved out – and left the home behind in a state of disrepair.

Now, the homeowner said he still cannot sell his own property.

Washington homeowner Ellis Cameron says a property manager he hired took over his rental home in the affluent community of Edgewood. (Ellis Cameron)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The homeowner wants others to see his story as a cautionary tale, urging people not to rent out their property in a blue state. He said he wishes he would have opted to rent out a property in a red state – where squatters can be criminally charged.

He said, "Florida's laws changed to get the squatters out and they [are] not only getting them out of there, but they [are] charging them criminally for squatting."

He went on to say, "They have the tougher laws there."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Earlier this year, expanded criminal penalties for squatters went into effect in Florida.

A before and after photo shows how an alleged squatter made a mess of a homeowner's property. (Ellis Cameron)

"You have to look at whenever you decide to rent your place out, what the laws are and where your house is," he said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson's Office and the Adelbai family for comment.
