title: Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge
excerpt:
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release.

Abu Safia’s lawyer s...
body_text:
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release.

Abu Safia’s lawyer said that a court in Beersheba decided on Wednesday to extend the physician’s detention for a further six months, according to Abu Safia’s account on X.

The court said that Abu Safia “poses a threat to the State of Israel”, his lawyer reported.

“Dr Hussam questioned why his detention order was being renewed once again, expressing that he is being punished for fulfilling his humanitarian mission and professional duty as a doctor at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza,” the social media post added.

The Israeli army detained Abu Safia in December 2024, along with other staff members and patients, during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza.

International agencies and rights groups have called for the physician’s release on multiple occasions, highlighting reports that he is being subjected to abuse in detention.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said in July that Israel “must immediately release Dr Abu Safiya, or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offence and grant him a fair trial”.

OHCHR added that it received information indicating Abu Safia “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care”.

Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said last week it had obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a significant loss of weight, a drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated.

“Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said.

Last week, the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking the release of 14 doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, who are being held in Israeli prisons without being charged or brought to trial.

PHRI argued that the prolonged arbitrary detentions – in some cases for more than two years – constitute a violation of their individual rights and further undermine Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical professionals.

title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’ in speech
excerpt:
Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin

Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

Xi Jinping tol...
body_text:
Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin

Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.

Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.

Xinhua reported the following remarks by the Chinese president:

double quotation markWhen I visited the United States in September this year, president Trump and his wife made a special trip to the airport to welcome me, and a grand welcoming ceremony was held.

China is a nation of courtesy, with a tradition of reciprocity. I welcome you back to China and look forward to exchanging in-depth views with you on major issues concerning China–US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape, so as to advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.”

Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin.

In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.

Xi also urged closer political and military ties between the two countries.
 
 
 He said “the two sides should leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties, ensuring that the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state is effectively implemented”, according to the readout.

In a notable gesture, Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.

As a reminder, Ukraine carried out a major strike on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, destroying its central road section in an operation involving two strikes over consecutive days.

The attack earlier this week dealt a significant blow to a key transport link and a symbolic project for Vladimir Putin, as the Russian president sat down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for talks at the Apec summit.

My colleague Jakub Krupa has the latest on the Ukraine conflict over on our Europe live blog here:

While we await Trump to disembark Air Force Once, we have this report from our China correspondent Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen:

Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age.

“Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.

In his address to the summit this morning, Putin had said that “the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.

Speaking at an outdoor press conference as purple clouds lingered ominously in the background, Carney said: “Not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on.”

Carney had previously said he would not boycott a group photo with Putin out of respect for hosts China. But he said if he were to find himself next to the Russian president, he would make Canada’s position clear.

Carney met China’s president Xi Jinping on Tuesday, with the two countries announcing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

The two men also discussed AI, Carney said Wednesday, adding he had taken the opportunity to share Canada’s views on a model for global governance.

“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” he said. “It’s an enormous economic risk but it’s a biohazard risk, and it’s a risk to democracy, human dignity, other factors... So it is past time to develop global governance frameworks for these sectors.”

Carney is due to meet Donald Trump later today, he said, where they would discuss efforts to reach a trade deal.

“We have been making progress... Two steps forward, one step back type thing,” he said.

He said he fully respected Trump’s engagement with China.

“I’m going to say something positive here about the initiative around denuclearization, the trilateral meeting that is going to happen,” he said. “Guess what? Canada’s in favor of denuclearization. If the relationship can be used towards that end, we’re very much supportive of it.”

Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Apec summit, Chinese state media reported.

The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has arrived in China for the Apec summit, Reuters reports, in her first official visit to the country since becoming the leader of Japan.

Like Trump, she also travelled from Manila, the Philippines, where she met with the leaders of the US, Australia and India as part of the Quad (a security grouping of the four countries) held in parallel with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).

As Trump makes his way to China, he has posted a message on his Truth Social platform reflecting on his visit to the Philippines and his meeting with president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

double quotation markI am now heading to China, from the Philippines, where we had a wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects. I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of “Energy.” President Marcos is a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance. It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son.”

Trump has suggested this week that he could meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China, but there has been no official confirmation from Beijing and Pyongyang has only published photos of its leader visiting a ski resort.

In case you missed it, here are those extraordinary photos:

US president Donald Trump pictured at Ninoy Aquino airport in Manila, the Philippines, pumping his fist as he boards Air Force One for Shenzhen, China, to attend the Apec summit.

Thanks for tuning into our live blog of the Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.

Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI. “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”

Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “former hegemons”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed ⁠after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.

Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.

The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for world order after the second world war and became shorthand for great power deals imposed on smaller countries.

It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.

Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just ⁠concluded a “very big ⁠trade ​deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila ⁠did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the ⁠biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it ​is a fair ‌deal for both countries,” ‌Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine ‌presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.

Donald Trump has said he doesn’t want to talk about Nvidia, the AI giant at the centre of a global espionage scandal, but AI will surely be on the agenda.

Countries have called for stronger governance and regulation of AI, as worries grow about its potential for military use and the risks posed by rogue autonomous-agent tools.

The China-US talks could build on the AI “communication channel” agreed when Trump and Xi met in Washington in September, Reuters reports.

double quotation markThe next step should be to agree on what constitutes a reportable incident, who has authority to communicate, how quickly notifications must occur and how information can be verified without disclosing sensitive capabilities,” said Marina Zhang from the University of Technology Sydney.

Media reports have also suggested Xi, Putin and Trump may discuss the use of AI in nuclear weapons command systems.

Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden and Xi had agreed in 2024 that any decision to use nuclear weapons should be controlled by humans, not by AI, the White House said.

Taiwan’s representative Stan Shih, founder of computer manufacturer Acer, is expected to arrive in Shenzhen with a delegation this morning.

Among the 21 Apec member economies, Taiwan’s participation is particularly sensitive, given that host country China claims the self-governing democracy as its territory.

Taiwan joined Apec in 1991 under the name “Chinese Taipei” and remains a full member despite its limited diplomatic recognition. Home to TSMC, the world’s leading contract chipmaker, the island plays a crucial role in the global supply of advanced semiconductors essential to AI, a key focus of discussions at the summit.

Ahead of the summit, China reiterated that Taiwan’s participation in Apec must adhere to its “one-China principle”, a position rejected by Taipei, which insists that its participation as a forum member is not subject to Beijing’s policy.

A Tuesday poll shows that 71.8% of respondents in Taiwan supported the government’s participation in the Shenzhen summit on “equal and dignified terms.”

Taiwan could also come up in talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday.

Asked on Tuesday whether Taiwan had communicated with Washington ahead of Trump’s talks with Chinese and Russian leaders, Taiwan’s foreign ministry spokesperson said communication channels with the US are “running smoothly” and the ministry is closely monitoring Trump’s meetings at the summit.

Trade tensions are likely to loom over the Apec summit this year, just a year after Trump and Xi Jinping reached a tenuous truce in their trade war on the sidelines of the last Apec summit in South Korea.

The leaders’ “priority” would be “keeping the truce alive”, especially with another Trump-Xi meeting expected at the G20 summit in Miami in December, said Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), as reported by Reuters.

Countries like Canada are also expected to be looking to broaden their trade partnerships – including with China – to reduce dependence on the United States.

Trump has of course upended global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on many countries.

Kim Jong-un had plenty to gain from his three meetings with Donald Trump during the US president’s first term in office.

Seven years on from their last meeting, along the heavily armed border dividing the Korean peninsula, speculation is mounting that the North Korean leader will end their estrangement at this week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen.

But some analysts are casting doubt on the likelihood of a fourth Trump-Kim meeting in the Chinese city.

After making rapid progress with his country’s nuclear and missile programmes and forming a loose “axis of upheaval” with Beijing and Moscow, what, they ask, would Kim have to gain from another encounter with his American counterpart?

Apec’s Chinese hosts say they have no information on a possible bilateral, while the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to play down the prospect, saying preparations for a dialogue between Kim and Trump did not mean it would happen.

Trump, who floated the idea just before leaving Washington on Monday, has raised the prospect of a resumption of nuclear diplomacy before, yet the men have not met since their brief meeting along the DMZ in June 2019, months after they failed to agree on how US would compensate Pyongyang for dismantling its nuclear arsenal.

Speculation that Kim would make an appearance alongside other world leaders increased, however, after a report by Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted the Kremlin as saying Vladimir Putin could meet Kim ⁠if he attended the Apec summit.

The Kremlin “wouldn’t do that unless they were certain he was going to meet”, Sydney Seiler, a former US national intelligence officer for North Korea, now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Reuters. “I’m pretty confident something’s underway.”

Others North Korea experts were more skeptical. Kim would have nothing to gain from a trip to Shenzhen except photo opportunities, said Kim Dong-yup, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Far East Institute. “Let’s say they offer to remove sanctions. But sanctions are already not working. There’s nothing to gain for Kim. Why would he go and open himself up to potential uncertainty?”

North Korean state media have been silent on the speculation. Official photos released this week showed a smiling Kim, accompanied by his wife and daughter, perched on an armchair in the snow at a ski resort near the North Korea-China border.

Wearing aviator shades, a cigarette dangling from his fingers, Kim did not give the impression he was ready to resurrect his “friendship” with a weakened US president.

As mentioned earlier, Zelenskyy is undeniably concerned about the Apec trilateral meeting between the Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andriy Sybiga said earlier this week that a meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders would “only encourage Putin to continue this war”.

Beijing has said the three leaders will discuss “safeguarding world peace”, but US officials say Trump is not expected to bring up Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Beijing, insisting it is a neutral party, has never denounced the Russian invasion, and has instead called for peace talks.

“Beijing will remain respectful of Russia’s own aims in the war and balance that with growing calls from Europe to exert a little more influence in that regard,” NTU’s Loh said, as reported by Reuters news agency.

Putin would probably have the most to gain from the trilateral meeting, ASPI’s Lee added.

double quotation markJust being at the table with Trump and Xi would elevate Russia’s standing and potentially shift the conversation toward a broader great-power bargain over European security.

title: Shabana Mahmood pledges to tackle ‘corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing’ – UK politics live
excerpt:
Home secretary to give speech to National Police Chiefs’ Council addressing concerns that officers treats groups differently

Good morning. Shabana Mahmood has done two of the most difficult jobs in t...
body_text:
Home secretary to give speech to National Police Chiefs’ Council addressing concerns that officers treats groups differently

Good morning. Shabana Mahmood has done two of the most difficult jobs in the government. With Labour under pressure from anti-migrant populists, in Reform UK, in the Conservative party and in the media, as justice secretary and home secretary she has been on the frontline in all the debates where the fight between the right and progressive politics has been most intensive. And she has developed a bold, novel, and largely successful strategy for winning these battles; she disarms her critics by agreeing with them.

Not entirely, of course. She is still a Labour cabinet minister. But sometimes she can sound a bit like Chris Philp.

And today we are going to get another example. In a speech to the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), she will tell officers that she wants to do something about so-called two-tier policing – the theory that, under pressure to be politically correct, the police have become biased towards leftwing causes and nervous about enforcing the law against minority ethnic people for fear of being seen as racist.

On the right, the existence of this version of two-tier policing is now an article of faith, even though most of the time actual policing is very different. This is how Robert Hutton from the Critic satirised the idea in a sketch two years ago, during 2024 summer riots when racists were trying to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers.

double quotation markThis is about fairness, Ed, and it’s a very important point. When I talk about two-tier policing, I’m talking about the way that different groups of marchers are treated. For instance, if you go to a Pride march, there are police with rainbow flags on their cars. During the Black Lives Matter protests, the police took the knee. But you go to these protests, and do you see the police waving swastikas? No you don’t. When was the last time you saw a film of a policeman kicking a brown-skinned person in the head? Well, OK, but when was the last time you saw a video of a policeman trying to set fire to a building full of refugees? Exactly. That’s what we mean by two-tier policing.

Here is a Guardian article looking at whether policing really is two-tier. In some respects, it is, the article points out. “Black people remained more likely than any other ethnic group to be subjected to almost every form of force, from handcuffing and dog bites to firearms and Tasers, when compared with population or arrest figures.”

In her speech today, from the extracts released in advance, Mahmood is not going to say that there is two-tier policing. But she will argue that it is important to respond to the “perception” it exists. She will say:

double quotation markWe must tackle head-on the corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing in this country.

Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed.

But there have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing people – often motivated actors – to whip up the idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.

In its report previewing the speech, the Press Association says:

double quotation markMahmood will lament the low levels of black officers in police forces, while also warning against “misguided attempts at course correction” that lead to “differential treatment”.

And she will warn officers against engaging with “activist groups”, telling them to “leave the politics to the politicians”.

She will also set out plans to fast-track talented recruits – including from outside policing – to senior ranks to address sometimes “inadequate” leadership.

A new “impartiality standard” is being developed to ensure all members of the public are treated equally, she will tell chief constables and police and crime commissioners.

This will bring guidance on key impartiality principles into one place and aims to give police more confidence in how they handle cases, regardless of someone’s race, faith or other characteristics, and to give the public confidence they will be treated fairly.

A third of Britons believe police treat people from ethnic minority backgrounds more favourably than white people, a More in Common poll found earlier this year, noting this marks a doubling in the last two years.

Mahmood will tell the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) that it is “shameful”, 33 years after the murder of black teenager Stephen Lawrence, that the proportion of black officers remains virtually unchanged.

But Mahmood will argue that some approaches intended to promote equality, such as the former police anti-racism commitment, have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing.

double quotation markWe must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing does not mean treating everyone the same.

This is a reference to the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, a document that has frequently been criticised by the Conservatives and Reform UK. It says producing equality of policing outcomes “does not mean treating everyone ‘the same’”.

9.30am: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, gives evidence to the Commons Northern Ireland committee.

11am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives a speech at the King’s Fund conference.

Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.

1pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives a speech on policing.

After 12.30pm: MPs begin a debate on a Tory opposition day motion opposing most of the key features of the PM’s proposed UK-EU reset deal due to be agreed on Friday.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

The Conservatives and Reform UK do not seem very impressed by Shabana Mahmood’s proposal to meet their concerns about two-tier policing.

This is from Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.

double quotation markIf you don’t want two-tier justice, stop legislating for it.

Two-tier justice comes from the equality duty, human rights laws, DEI policies, differential sentencing policies, conscious choices like the “Islamophobia” definition, the decision to use the Public Order Act as a de facto blasphemy law, the deliberate decision not to enforce the law during the anti-Israel marches, appointing communalist interests to police and CPS advisory boards, and more.

The issue is not training the police to treat people equally - it’s all the decisions that stop the criminal justice system treating us as equal before the law.

And this is from Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markLast year the Home Office believed claims of “two-tier” policing were “far-right”. Will they now apologise?

Even in her statement Mahmood still can’t bring herself to say it’s wrong.

Lucy Powell, the Labour deputy leader, has criticised media organisations for playing a message from rapist comedian Russell Brand.

As the Press Association reports, Brand’s wife Laura Gallacher shared the message from the jailed sex offender in which he insisted he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year term. Gallacher read out the message on a YouTube podcast on Sunday, prompting an official investigation into whether Brand has breached prison rules.

Asked about this in an interview on LBC this morning, Powell said:

double quotation markI was appalled at that and actually I think mainstream media shouldn’t have transmitted that either.

Brand was “someone who’s not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims”, she said.

double quotation markThis is somebody who’s been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape.

Asked why she wanted to censor that message, she said: “It’s a platform I don’t think … should have been amplified, to be honest.”

Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”, Nadeem Badshaw and Kiran Stacey report.

In his Today interview, David Lammy also said that he would not be standing to be Labour’s next candidate for mayor of London. He said he was still enjoying national politics. There had been speculation that he might apply if Sadiq Khan decided not to stand for a fourth term in 2028. Today voting ends in the Tory election to choose their candidate and James Cleverly (like Lammy, a former foreign secretary), is expected to win.

Khan had been expected not to seek a fourth term. But, with Andy Burnham beefing up the powers available to mayors, making the job more attractive, there is increasing speculation that he will try to stay on.

David Lammy was on the Today programme this morning talking about his call for the UK to rejoin the EU. (See 9.49am.) Asked about Shabana Mahmood’s speech on two-tier policing (see 9.04am), Lammy, a former justice secretary, replied:

double quotation markI don’t think that there’s two-tier policing in Britain.

But I think there’s a preception [of two-tier policing] because of too many guidelines that are not straightforward. If [Shabana Mahmood] is tidying that up – I haven’t seen the detail [of her speech later] – then I would welcome that.

David Lammy, the former foreign secretary and former deputy PM, has used an article in the Times to say that Andy Burnham should proposing rejoining the EU in the next Labour manifesto. He says:

double quotation markBurnham has to show how joining the EU passes the Makerfield test. I believe to do that it should answer three questions. What will deliver the most growth? What will deliver the most security? And what will help prevent uncontrolled irregular migration?

The customs union doesn’t deliver major growth on its own. The single market without EU membership gives Britain economic growth but with little influence over the rules we follow. Only membership answers all three questions. On migration, it would put Britain back inside the EU’s asylum returns system, giving us access to the tools we lost in 2020 and have only been rebuilding piecemeal ever since. The ability for Brits to live and work in Europe and Europeans to live and work in Britain with free movement would return. But I believe, like Ireland, we can remain outside Schengen, and, like Sweden, we can stay out of the eurozone.

Burnham’s Labour should go into the next election clear that its intention is to rejoin the EU. Forming the next government would give it the mandate to begin formal negotiations. Once a deal is agreed, this should be put to the people against the status quo. Unlike the last referendum, the public should have the opportunity to decide between two clearly defined choices.

Lammy also says, towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, he tried to get Starmer to agree to abandon Labour’s red lines on Europe (ruling out rejoining, or joining the single market or customs union) at the next election. But Starmer resisted, he suggests.

Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households, Jillian Ambrose reports.

Here is another quote from what Shabana Mahmood will say in her speech to the the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC).

double quotation markCommunity engagement should mean going to a residents’ association meeting and discussing local issues. It can be over tea and biscuits, or tea and samosas, but it doesn’t mean engaging with activist groups and campaigners who are pushing an agenda and not representing a community.

Leave the politics to the politicians – and we will leave the policing to you.

And here is Emine Sinmaz’s story about this.

title: Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
excerpt: A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators ...
body_text:
A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators warning the report could help justify further attacks on civilian facilities.

The controversy comes as Washington threatens renewed military action against Iran, following months of war that have already left the country’s energy facilities, bridges, water infrastructure and other civilian sites damaged.

“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a post on X.

The newspaper has defended its reporting, insisting it accurately represented the views of its experts.

However, several experts quoted by the publication have publicly challenged the implications of the investigation, questioning the evidence behind the proposed link between dams and military installations.

The controversy has also revived memories of the NYT’s reporting in the lead-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, when the paper’s journalists helped amplify claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that later proved unfounded.

Published on Tuesday, the story, headlined “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason”, examined whether Iran’s extensive network of dams, pipelines and water-transfer projects could be connected to its underground missile programme.

The report cited researchers who observed geographical similarities between the locations of dams and sites targeted by US and Israeli air strikes.

According to the report, some of the water and military experts the NYT spoke to concluded that the “water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup”.

However, the newspaper itself acknowledged, “Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.”

Critics fear that portraying dams as potentially serving military purposes could provide a justification for attacking infrastructure essential to millions of civilians.

US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have damaged oil facilities, power plants, water reservoirs, bridges, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened further attacks, saying last week that key Iranian infrastructure could be destroyed within three days.

Political analyst Rami Khouri called the NYT report “troubling”, saying it reaffirmed his concerns about US mainstream media being “complicit in the US-Israeli criminal attacks on Iran, just as it was during the war on Iraq decades ago and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”.

“The telltale sign of non-credible wobbly journalism is when conditional words like ‘speculative’, ‘suggestive’, ‘may have developed’, ‘may shed light’, ‘suspect’, and ‘long-term riddle’ occur more often than any definitive, evidence-based facts.”

Khouri said it was “not definitive and verified reporting” and “another attempt to support the US-Israeli urgency to find any reason to carry out more war crimes against Iran” by attacking critical infrastructure.

“Another sad day for US mainstream journalism,” he added.

Aside from online criticism from readers and commentators, experts cited in the story have themselves come out against aspects of the report.

Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University’s water institute and a former senior Iranian environmental official, one of the experts cited in the story, challenged the report’s reasoning.

“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” he wrote on X.

“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles! This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure. The New York Times should know better.”

Madani also questioned the newspaper’s claim that seven experts had supported its analysis. “I’m one of the people quoted in the article, but my comments had nothing to do with dams or missiles!” he added.

Nima Shokri, a water-security expert at Hamburg University of Technology, whose research featured prominently in the investigation, also issued a clarification.

“The proximity of dams to military targets does not establish why those dams were built, nor does it justify attacks on them,” he said on X.

A third researcher quoted in the article echoed Shokri’s comments.

“I fully agree [with Shokri],” Amir Aghakouchak, a water expert at the University of California, Irvine, wrote on X, sharing Shokri’s X post.

“Dams and water infrastructure are essential to civilian life and must never become targets of military attacks. Regardless of their location or potential strategic significance, their primary roles in water supply, food security, energy, and environmental sustainability must not be overlooked. Protecting these critical resources should be a priority, regardless of politics or conflict.”

The newspaper rejected accusations that its investigation could provide a pretext for military attacks.

“Our report on Iranian dams accurately cited research and analysis by seven international experts on Iran’s environment and military presence,” spokesperson Nicole Taylor said.

She added that the NYT’s journalists had sought to explain Iran’s infrastructure investment and the effects of US and Israeli attacks on civilians.

“Framing the independent reporting as a pretext for violence is dangerous,” Taylor said.

One of the story’s co-authors, Sanam Mahoozi, said that “neither I nor our report endorses or justifies attacks on dams or other infrastructure”.

“As a journalist, I welcome rigorous, constructive criticism, but I hope some users will critique the report fairly, based on what was actually written,” she posted on X. The story was co-written with Erika Solomon, the NYT bureau chief for Iraq and Iran.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish”, accusing what he suggested was pro-Israel media of promoting narratives reminiscent of the run-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.

“Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it,” he wrote on X.

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, accused the newspaper of preparing the ground for further attacks on civilian infrastructure.

“New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” he posted on X.

The controversy has revived widespread criticism of the newspaper’s reporting before the US-led invasion of Iraq, when claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction helped build public support for war.

Judith Miller, a former NYT journalist, was among the reporters whose coverage amplified claims about Iraq’s weapons programmes that subsequently proved unfounded.

In September 2002, Miller co-authored a report claiming Iraq had intensified its pursuit of nuclear weapons, citing US officials who alleged that Baghdad was seeking aluminium tubes for uranium enrichment.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney cited the newspaper’s reporting on aluminium tubes to bolster President George W Bush’s administration’s case against Iraq. The claims were later discredited.

Two months after the invasion of Iraq began in March 2003, Miller co-authored a report citing that US intelligence agencies had concluded that two mysterious trailers found in Iraq were mobile units to “produce germs for weapons”.

However, a year after the US war on Iraq began, the NYT acknowledged serious shortcomings in its reporting on the build-up to war, including its reliance on Iraqi defectors and exiles seeking regime change.

“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” it said.

title: Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
excerpt:
Khartoum, Sudan – Mohammed Awad never imagined that his life would change so dramatically when war broke out in his home city of Khartoum in April 2023 when he was aged 17.

He found himself displaced...
body_text:
Khartoum, Sudan – Mohammed Awad never imagined that his life would change so dramatically when war broke out in his home city of Khartoum in April 2023 when he was aged 17.

He found himself displaced and forced out of school, moving from one state to another accompanied by his cousins and searching for a safe place where he could escape the horrors of war.

But what began as a journey in search of safety became the beginning of a personal tragedy, one experienced by millions of people in Sudan who are in the midst of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in which killing and displacement have become routine.

“I started taking drugs to forget what I have seen and the horrors I have been through in Khartoum during the first months of the war. My friends and my cousin were killed in front of me,” he told Al Jazeera. “I am trying to recover now, so I can proceed with my education and life.”

The conflict between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group saw the capital become one of the initial epicentres of this power struggle between the two former military allies.

The war trapped thousands of people in Khartoum State in their homes for weeks or forced them to flee, but since the SAF expelled the RSF from the region in May last year, it has now become a haven for millions of people fleeing fighting elsewhere in Sudan. The war has led to a humanitarian catastrophe with at least 59,000 people killed and 14 million people forced to leave their homes in a country with a population of 52 million. Displacement is more than the simple act of moving from one place to another but a journey marked by fear, anxiety and instability with increasingly limited options in life.

For those such as Awad caught in the pressures of displacement and the absence of a supportive environment, drugs have become a way of dealing with an unbearable reality.

“I entered rehabilitation centres many times, and I quickly returned to addiction. I take pills and sometimes weed. I want to stop, but I keep failing over and over again,” Awad said.

The war in Sudan has not only severely impacted individual civilians’ lives but has also torn apart the social fabric of the country. The lack of security and poverty have also led to a proliferation of drugs manufacturing and trade, particularly the highly addictive amphetamine Captagon. According to government officials, areas currently or formerly under RSF control are a particular problem.

The Qadreen Center for Addiction Treatment is one of the few charitable institutions dealing with the problem in Khartoum, and doctors in the capital told Al Jazeera there is growing demand for their services.

“The centre continues to provide its medical services both before and after the outbreak of the war,” the centre’s director, Lubna Ali, said.

“Following the war, it witnessed a significant increase in the number of cases seeking treatment amid growing needs for mental health and addiction recovery services.”

Since the war has broken out, the centre has treated 10,100 cases ranging from patients in need of psychological support for war-related trauma to those with drug addiction. Ali said 135 such individuals have been treated “in their recovery journey”.

Young people are particularly affected by the war, witnessing horrific violence, displacement, the loss of friends and relatives, interrupted education and quickly declining employment opportunities.

Weakened institutions and a deteriorating security situation have undermined oversight efforts and the ability of health services to respond to the addiction crisis.

Dr Aisha Almobasher, a psychiatrist at the Bitmakaly National Organization, which provides psychological and therapeutic support to individuals affected by war and addiction, told Al Jazeera that some areas of Sudan are worse affected by the drug problem than others.

“The growing number of people seeking treatment suggests that this is more than a passing phenomenon. Many of those struggling with addiction come from areas previously controlled by the Rapid Support Forces, RSF, where, following their withdrawal, drugs reportedly became more widely available and trafficking networks expanded,” she told Al Jazeera.

“In some states, drugs also became a means of attracting and recruiting young people, particularly into the ranks of RSF fighters, drawing many of them onto a dark path.”

According to a report published by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker in March, 19 incidents involving the seizures of drugs or manufacturing facilities were recorded in Sudan from 2015 to 2025 with a notable acceleration since the outbreak of the war.

These figures refer to seizures and estimated production capacity not actual drug consumption. Nevertheless, they reveal the scale of the problem and the transformation taking place in the country’s illicit drug trade.

Major-General (Legal) Mohamed Al-Moatasim Okasha, director of Sudan’s General Directorate for Anti-Narcotics, said its teams have dealt with an increase in drug manufacturing and production since the war began.

They have found advanced drug production facilities in areas retaken from the RSF by the SAF, including areas in and around Khartoum. El-Radom, an area in South Darfur State in western Sudan, has become a well-known cannabis-growing region, he said.

“It remains under RSF control and is expected to return to the control of the Sudanese armed forces soon. Throughout the past three years of war, antinarcotics operations in this area have been suspended with no other authority able to effectively address the problem due to its inaccessibility under RSF control,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Meanwhile, the use and circulation of other narcotic substances have been increasing, particularly Captagon, crystal methamphetamine (ice) and drugs such as tramadol. However, these substances remain less widespread than cannabis and other traditionally prevalent drugs.”

A huge facility for manufacturing Captagon pills was recently discovered by the SAF north of Khartoum, close to an oil refinery that was formerly under RSF control.

SAF forces uncovered drugs manufacturing equipment valued at about $3m. The facility was capable of producing 100,000 Captagon pills per hour with raw materials potentially able to produce 700 million pills.

“These are not merely allegations of drug trafficking, smuggling or distribution. They are evidence of industrial-scale drug production taking place in areas that were under RSF control,” Okasha told Al Jazeera.

“As for drug use among combatants, there have been reports and testimonies indicating that quantities of narcotic substances were found in the possession of captured militia members. This highlights how widespread these substances have become and how readily accessible they are to fighters.”

Drug trafficking and manufacturing have become weapons of war, not just illicit sources of income, and they are directly impacting the conflict between the SAF and RSF, he said. Captagon has become a regional issue with facilities producing the drug in Syria during the rule of former President Bashar al-Assad flooding the illicit market.

While the new government in Damascus is trying to crack down on these facilities in southern Syria, Captagon production is a growing problem in other regional conflict areas such as Sudan.

“Sudan faces this growing threat amid the ongoing conflict,” Okasha said. “Through strong nationwide coordination, we are intensifying seizures and disrupting smuggling, trafficking and production networks. Our mission is to stop the spread of narcotics, protect our youth and safeguard future generations. Combating drugs is a national security priority.”

“The drug problem in Sudan cannot be viewed in isolation. It is a regional challenge, and Sudan is part of a region experiencing a growing drug crisis.”

title: GOP chairman demands answers on Trump's costly VA technology overhaul amid US-wide outages
excerpt:
President Donald Trump highlights his administration's efforts to reform the Department of Veterans Affairs, including expanding veterans' healthcare choices and strengthening VA accountability.

Shif...
body_text:
President Donald Trump highlights his administration's efforts to reform the Department of Veterans Affairs, including expanding veterans' healthcare choices and strengthening VA accountability.

Shifting timelines and ballooning costs of the Trump administration's contracts to modernize the federal government, including programs affecting veterans, are raising alarm bells on Capitol Hill.

House Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost, R-Ill., wrote to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) this month asking for more information on an Oracle software rollout for streamlining employee data and what, if any, safeguards are in place to stop potential data breaches from leaking Americans' sensitive personal information. It comes as the country has grappled with multiple outages hitting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), big banks, and Microsoft, among other entities.

"I write to you today to express concern about the pace of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Federal Human Resources (HR) 2.0 implementation, uncertainty surrounding VA’s transition costs and readiness, and the risks posed by another major Oracle implementation affecting the Department," the letter said.

"The House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs supports efforts to modernize HR systems and improve how VA manages and supports its workforce. However, modernization must proceed with clear accountability, adequate resources, and safeguards against disruption."

‘BIG BALLS’ OF DOGE FAME GIVES EXCLUSIVE LOOK AT NEW TRUMP MISSION TO OVERHAUL GOVERNMENT

Illinois Republican Rep. Mike Bost speaks alongside Rep. Lisa McClain, a Republican from Michigan, and Rep. Steve Scalise, a Republican from Louisiana, during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Technology firm Cerner won a $10 billion government contract in 2018 to modernize record-keeping at VA-run hospitals over 10 years. Cerner was acquired by multinational tech company Oracle four years later.

ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS

It was later paused for several years during the Biden administration in an effort to root out performance issues affecting veterans and healthcare providers at VA hospitals, the department said at the time.

Since then, the VA announced earlier this year it would extend that contract through 2031 — with a new total price tag of $27 billion.

OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS

It's raised concerns among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, including Bost, who referenced those issues in his questions on the VA's use of Oracle for modernizing its employee data via HR 2.0.

"More than four months after Oracle was selected to provide the governmentwide platform underpinning HR 2.0, the Committee seeks detailed evidence of implementation progress and readiness at VA. In addition, VA’s years-long experience with Oracle’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program reinforces the need for caution," Bost wrote.

A Department of Veterans Affairs sign is displayed outside the Washington VA Medical Center on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Bost also cited system performance issues and problems with user satisfaction with EHRM highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), but he said only four of GAO's 18 recommendations have been fully implemented as of this past August.

In June 2026, Oracle was awarded a $395.8 million contract to modernize the federal government's human resources systems.

DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

An independent government watchdog "identified inconsistent completion targets, concentrated security and authorization risk, vendor-dependent data migration, and persistent staffing gaps" with HR 2.0 software implementation in October, Bost noted.

"The report describes completion targets shifting from July 4, 2027, to as late as March 2028, while the Wave 2 timeline remains unset," he wrote.

He also raised concerns about the potential for a data breach after the FBI was targeted by hackers in September.

Though he noted existing reports about that hack do not link it to potential issues with Oracle's software at the VA, Bost suggested that staffing gaps and HR 2.0's "centralized authorization approach" could allow for vulnerabilities that need to be accounted for before the rollout is complete.

Fears of tech vulnerabilities are at an all-time high in the U.S. after multiple private and public entities experienced disruptions in service. Travelers were hit with chaos last week after an issue with air traffic control towers caused a nationwide ground stop of flights, while Amtrak's booking system also went offline for several hours.

Just on Monday, major banks like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America experienced some service disruptions and transaction delays.

The incidents have not been connected so far.

In his letter, Bost also called on more transparency with HR 2.0's funding, warning it should not take away from resources aimed at Oracle's contract on veterans' healthcare systems.

"Identify VA’s projected costs, savings, funding sources, and funding gaps for fiscal years 2027 through 2029," Bost asked. "Explain how OPM and the VA will protect resources needed for EHRM and veterans’ services, avoid duplicative implementation spending, and ensure timely retirement of legacy systems."

When reached for comment, an OPM official told Fox News Digital the office "is working closely with agencies and stakeholders throughout implementation to drive adoption, manage change effectively, and continuously improve the platform over time. We take concerns over data security seriously and also want to highlight that HCM will be leveraging Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, not PeopleSoft."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
excerpt:
Energy firm says existing market arrangements do not sustain facility’s continued operation

The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England...
body_text:
Energy firm says existing market arrangements do not sustain facility’s continued operation

The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England next summer, if the government does not intervene to offer support amid weak market conditions.

The site, located near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, consists of eight caverns with the capacity to store about 309m cubic metres of gas, estimated at about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage.

SSE said in an update to investors: “It is increasingly clear that existing market arrangements do not support their continued operation.”

It added that gas storage facilities such as Atwick have a “strategic importance” to the energy system.

Energy companies rely on stockpiling gas in their storage facilities during the summer, when demand is lower and prices are usually lower, before withdrawing the stored gas and selling it during winter when demand for energy for heating and power peaks.

However, the gas price increase triggered by the Iran conflict and the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz have made it uneconomical to stockpile gas during the summer.

As a result, countries across Europe have entered the cooler months of the year with gas stores at their lowest level in more than a decade.

SSE said: “Despite current commodity prices, favourable spreads are not emerging to support the ongoing commercial operation of Atwick.” It came as the company announced its results for the six months to the end of September.

The closure of a gas storage facility such as Atwick could leave the UK even more exposed to price shocks on global markets.

Britain already stores less gas than some of its European neighbours and is instead more reliant on liquefied natural gas imports.

SSE’s announcement comes months after British Gas’s owner, Centrica, warned it would close its Rough site – the UK’s largest gas storage facility – unless it can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government.

The trade union Unite has called on ministers and Centrica to work together to secure the future of Rough, which the company has scheduled for closure in April 2027.

SSE said it continued to engage with the government “on the need for policy intervention to support a resilient gas system”.

The Atwick facility has been in operation since 1979 and has been owned by SSE since September 2002.

The jump in wholesale gas prices has fed through into household bills. On Wednesday the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the typical household gas and electricity bill will jump by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year.

The government has been contacted for comment.

title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
excerpt:
Mary Peltola defeated the state's Republican incumbent after a controversial race

Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US...
body_text:
Mary Peltola defeated the state's Republican incumbent after a controversial race

Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.

Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.

Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.

Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.

Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?

Could Alaska's fishing industry tilt Washington's balance of power?

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times, external reported that her team worked with people who tried to recruit so-called spoiler candidates in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

The alleged scheme led to a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan - a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan - contesting the race.

After legal challenges, state courts ruled that Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.

Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the US justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.

The Trump administration also filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.

A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.

Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could have simply chosen both men, listing them as their first and second choices.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would have re-allocated any votes from Daniel J Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to Dan S Sullivan.

Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.

An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for Daniel J Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, Peltola would still have won.

The Democratic win in Alaska cements the party's majority in the US Senate, as the party now has 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.

The most senior Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said Peltola had run "a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about". Hailing the Democrats' final tally in the Senate, he said: "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago."

The Alaska seat was initially one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the US Senate. But by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50% of the votes, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.

Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.

Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.

"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state

Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections

title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high
excerpt:
Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January

Inflation in t...
body_text:
Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.

As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate.

“Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices respectively.”

Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global increase in energy prices.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2.p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.

At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20 million households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.

The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October.

A new forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.

A spokesperson for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The MPC raised bank rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there.”

Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could be forced to raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.

Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.

Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.

Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.

Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.

“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.

“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”

title: Dem governor’s tale of mourning fellow serviceman ripped apart after soldiers wife gives brutal fact check
excerpt:
Fox News Digital spoke to Retired Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling who pushed back against Moore’s claims that he "led paratroopers in combat" in Afghanistan.

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore – widely be...
body_text:
Fox News Digital spoke to Retired Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling who pushed back against Moore’s claims that he "led paratroopers in combat" in Afghanistan.

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore – widely believed to be seriously weighing a presidential run in 2028 – is facing controversy yet again over his characterization of his military record, this time facing allegations he embellished his relationship with a fallen soldier and used an impossible timeline to tell an emotional story in his memoir.

The issue stems from a Baltimore Sun report over the weekend highlighting a passage in Moore's 2015 book, "The Work: Searching for a Life That Matters," where he told the story of breaking into tears at his grandfather's funeral when hearing about the death of his friend Tobias "Toby" Meister.

"Inside that casket, I also saw Toby," Moore wrote in his book, adding that he cried for his grandfather, Toby, and other fallen soldiers.

MARYLAND GOV WES MOORE IN HOT SEAT AFTER REPORT QUESTIONS CLAIM ABOUT GRANDFATHER AND KKK

Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.) appears on "Meet the Press" in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 7, 2025. (Shannon Finney/NBC via Getty Images))

However, Moore's grandfather's funeral was on Dec. 17, 2005. Meister was killed in a roadside bombing 11 days later, on Dec. 28, 2005.

Moore did not learn about Meister's death until January of the next year, when he returned to Afghanistan, the Baltimore Sun reported.

After Meister's death, his wife Alicia told the outlet that many of his friends from the military have reached out to her over the years and keep his memory alive with their son, who was just over a year old when his father was killed.

A group of soldiers patrols in Afghanistan. (Getty Images Creatives)

"I’ve never heard from him," his wife Alicia told the outlet. "I’ve never personally heard from him," she added. "I don’t know who [Moore] is. I don’t recall my late husband ever talking about him."

WES MOORE CONFRONTED ON REPORTED MISREPRESENTATIONS ABOUT MISSING OXFORD THESIS, STORY ABOUT GREAT-GRANDFATHER

Days after the Baltimore Sun reached out to Moore's office for comment, Alicia Meister said she heard from Moore.

"It was good," she told the outlet. "He paid his respects and apologized for not reaching out sooner."

She added, "I do wish, though, that my late husband would be removed from the situation completely. I just don’t like that he has been brought in the middle of it."

Fox News Digital reached out to Moore's office for comment.

Moore previously acknowledged the conflicting timeline in interviews with the Baltimore Banner in June, attributing the inaccuracy to poor editing and the effects of stress, grief and time on his memory.

Chelsea Clinton and Gov. Wes Moore speak onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative)

In a lengthy response in the New York Post, a Moore spokesperson rejected the allegations as a "political hit job," saying that Moore knew and worked with Meister in Afghanistan and that fellow service members had corroborated their relationship. The spokesperson accused Sinclair executive chairman David Smith of exploiting a grieving Gold Star family to attack the governor and alleged the outlet misrepresented Moore’s willingness to be interviewed.

The report comes on the heels of a Baltimore Sun story earlier this month in which his former Army supervisor questioned the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat, a story told in the same book.

In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, the Baltimore Sun spoke with retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas.

SGT Matthew Taylor from Orlando, Florida, 1LT Wes Brockbank from Seattle, Washington and CPL Matthew Moebes from Decatur, Alabama with the U.S. Army's 4th Squadron 2d Cavalry Regiment walk through a village during a joint patrol with Afghan National Army soldiers near Kandahar, Afghanistan, on March 2, 2014. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Additionally, a New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.
