title: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
excerpt:
The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza.

In i...
body_text:
The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza.

In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse.

“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained.

The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza.

Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.

In recent weeks, Israel has continued to carry out deadly air strikes, and its ongoing restrictions have prevented the delivery of life-saving aid into Gaza ahead of the winter season.

“Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the board said in its report.

According to the board, the widespread devastation in Gaza has left Palestinians facing “another winter in tents and rubble”.

Trump first proposed the Board of Peace in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.

The board’s mission was laid out in a 20-point Gaza peace plan, as well as the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire formally began on October 10, 2025, though attacks have continued since.

The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.

But in Tuesday’s report, the board said Israel and Hamas have fallen far short of their commitments in the ceasefire deal.

“A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”

The board also noted that Israel has blocked the technocratic civil administration body created to run Gaza on an interim basis.

“The absence of decisions by the government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan,” the report said.

“The Board of Peace calls on the government of Israel to take these decisions without delay.”

To break the deadlock, the board called on the UN Security Council to press both sides to fulfil their agreements.

“Neither party may treat the other’s delay as license for its own inaction, and together these obligations are the only route to Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction at scale,” the report said.

It also added that the outcome must establish a credible path towards Palestinian statehood and self-determination, warning that no unilateral actions should be permitted to derail that ultimate goal.

title: Antonio Sabàto Jr and Virginia Madsen’s son bails himself out of jail after fatal hit-and-run in Alaska
excerpt:
Jack Sabàto allegedly struck 42-year-old Carl Simmonds while delivering for DoorDash and fled without stopping.

Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son, Jack Sabàto, has bailed himself out of ja...
body_text:
Jack Sabàto allegedly struck 42-year-old Carl Simmonds while delivering for DoorDash and fled without stopping.

Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son, Jack Sabàto, has bailed himself out of jail after being arrested in an Alaska hit-and-run that resulted in a fatality.

In court records reviewed by Fox News Digital, Jack paid bond of $5,000 Nov. 13 and was released Monday.

The 32-year-old was reportedly released under strict conditions prohibiting him from driving, sitting in the driver’s seat of a vehicle and possessing car keys, according to Page Six.

ANTONIO SABATO JR AND VIRGINIA MADSEN'S SON ARRESTED IN FATAL HIT-AND-RUN

Jack Sabàto posted bond of $5,000 after being arrested for his involvement with a fatal hit-and-run in Alaska. (Getty Images; KTUU)

Jack was arrested Nov. 9 on charges of leaving an accident without assisting the injured and leaving an accident resulting in injury or death, according to the Anchorage Police Department.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Police identified the victim as Carl Simmonds, 42, who was pronounced dead after officers and medics responded to reports of an unresponsive man near Airport Heights Drive and Debarr Road around 5:48 a.m. A preliminary investigation indicated a vehicle struck Simmonds and fled, police said.

FORMER PENN STATE FOOTBALL PLAYER FACES LIFE-ALTERING INJURIES AFTER HIT-AND-RUN CRASH THAT KILLED HIS FIANCÉE

Virginia Madsen and Antonio Sabàto Jr.'s son, Jack, was arrested Nov. 9. (Getty Images)

According to court records obtained by Fox News Digital, Jack faces a felony charge of leaving an accident without helping the victim and a misdemeanor charge of leaving an accident involving injury or death.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Charging documents reviewed by Alaska Public Media reported that responding officers found Simmonds' body on the sidewalk off Airport Heights Drive and several car parts scattered around.

While reviewing security footage from a nearby bank, officers saw a white Chevy Tahoe striking Simmonds and not braking before or after the crash, according to the outlet.

Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen share one son, Jack.  (Getty Images)

After running the vehicle’s description into the Alaska Public Safety Information Network, law enforcement found the matching vehicle, which is registered to Jack, parked at the Anchorage Amazon warehouse. The vehicle was seized.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

According to the charging documents, Jack told police he struck "something" while driving home after delivering for DoorDash, damaging his headlights. He said he believed he hit an animal and didn’t stop because he was driving without insurance. He also said he ran a red light because he felt unsafe driving without headlights.

He said he planned to report the crash after work but contacted police after his girlfriend told him his SUV had been seized, saying he "knew the worst," according to the documents.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

title: White House pulls Trump’s FDA pick Heidi Overton on eve of Senate panel vote
excerpt:
Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur debate whether the progressive challenge against Chuck Schumer signals a fractured Democratic Party or a routine internal disagreement.

The White Ho...
body_text:
Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur debate whether the progressive challenge against Chuck Schumer signals a fractured Democratic Party or a routine internal disagreement.

The White House pulled Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed to Fox News, one day before a Senate committee vote.

President Donald Trump hailed Overton as a "ROCKSTAR" in August when he picked the physician and White House advisor to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned in May.

At her September confirmation hearing, Overton clashed with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as he pressed her to endorse universal healthcare as a human right.

TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER

Heidi Overton, deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House Aug. 10, 2026. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, R-La., pointed to Overton’s appearance alongside Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.

Cassidy said there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

Dr. Heidi Overton answers questions during her confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C.

"Yes, Senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy. When he pressed her on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she hadn’t corrected Trump in the Oval Office.

NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

"So why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.

Overton worked on several of the administration’s Make America Healthy Again initiatives as a White House advisor.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS EMBRACE HEALTH AGENDA WHILE RATING RFK JR NEGATIVELY

President Donald Trump, joined by (L-R) National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, The Conservateur’s Jayme Leagh Franklin, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Deputy Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy Dr. Heidi Overton, after signing an executive order updating childhood vaccine recommendations on August 10, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Before returning to the White House, she served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the conservative America First Policy Institute, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.

Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.

PRO-LIFE CEO PREDICTS TRUMP FDA NOMINEE COULD BRING RENEWED SCRUTINY TO ABORTION DRUG RISKS

Erik Baptist, senior vice president for legal strategy at SBA Pro-Life America, said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs and changing how the agency studies their safety before the Senate holds a confirmation vote.

MAJOR PRO-LIFE GROUP THREATENS TO SUE TRUMP FDA OVER ABORTION PILL'S ALLEGED ENVIRONMENTAL RISKS"The administration must immediately end the Biden FDA’s mail-order abortion-drug scheme and protect pregnant women from predators who coerce or poison women with these drugs," Baptist said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And the FDA must fix its flawed safety study by obtaining robust data, increasing real-time transparency, and inviting external experts to help with this study."

"Confirmation is not a coronation," he added. "It is a time to vet nominees and seek commitments before they take office."

Fox News’ Pat Ward, Caroline McKee, and James Cirrone contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Sherrill commits $20.2M to deportation defense while condemning Rutgers over Border Patrol speaker
excerpt: Retired U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino is seen during his time leading border enforcement operations. Gov. Mikie Sherrill condemned Rutgers University’s College Republicans for inviting Bovin...
body_text:
Retired U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino is seen during his time leading border enforcement operations. Gov. Mikie Sherrill condemned Rutgers University’s College Republicans for inviting Bovino to speak on campus this week. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill put her money where her mouth was this week as the Democrat criticized Rutgers University’s College Republican chapter for hosting a top former Border Patrol leader around the same time her administration allocated millions to a program meant to help illegal immigrants and others in the state fight deportation.

Sherrill’s condemnation of the Rutgers students’ event drew criticism on X from observers who said it fueled protests outside the New Brunswick building where retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino spoke. Protests erupted inside the room as well, with video from inside showing Bovino responding to shouting protesters before he was briefly led out of the forum.

"Everyone in this country is entitled to due process and a fair hearing under the law — regardless of where they were born," Sherrill said Friday in announcing a total of $20.2 million to fund the Detention Deportation Defense Initiative within Trenton’s Office of New Americans.

NJ TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK FOR $12M MORE AS DEM GOVERNOR PROTECTS ILLEGAL ALIENS BATTLING DEPORTATION

Some of the funds will help migrants held at Delaney Hall in Essex County, where nightly protests have erupted since May. The governor previously visited the facility in solidarity with the detainees inside, while Sherrill ally Sen. Andy Kim, D-N. J., drew widespread attention online after being caught in a cloud of pepper spray dispersed by ICE toward surrounding protesters.

"With the Trump Administration ramping up ICE activity and creating impossible obstacles for people facing detention and deportation to navigate alone, New Jersey is stepping up to connect residents with qualified legal counsel and equip more attorneys to take on this vital work," Sherrill said Friday, adding that the state’s immigrant community should not have to face a "complex" legal system alone.

Commissioner Stephen Cha, head of Sherrill’s Department of Human Services, where the Office of New Americans sits, added in a statement that access to legal representation upholds due process and promotes a more "efficient" immigration system.

The $20.2 million will be spread among 10 service providers and continue the Murphy-era initiative’s mission to offer legal expertise and representation for "low-income residents facing detention and deportation."

EXCLUSIVE VIDEO: DEMS SLAMMED FOR DEMANDING ‘FIVE-STAR ACCOMMODATIONS’ FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AT ICE FACILITY

Protesters yell at then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino and federal agents during an earlier immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota. Protests also erupted inside and outside a Rutgers University building when Bovino spoke there Monday. (Armando L. Sanchez/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Sherrill’s new cash infusion tripled the initiative’s most recent budget allocation.

After Sherrill announced plans in June to increase the deportation defense initiative’s funding, Republicans in the state warned that the money could be better spent elsewhere, including on New Jersey residents.

"New Jersey families are being crushed by some of the highest electric bills, property taxes, and costs of living in the entire country, and Governor Sherrill's answer is to spend more than $20 million defending illegal immigrants," said outgoing Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who was unseated by Cape May Mayor Zachary Mullock in this month’s blue wave.

"It is a complete insult to every hardworking taxpayer in this state. New Jersey citizens should come first. If they can find $20 million for immigration lawyers, they can find money to lower utility delivery charges or provide relief to the people who actually live, work and pay taxes here."

Van Drew said in June that every dollar Trenton spends on an illegal immigrant is a dollar that could have helped keep a New Jersey family from leaving the state.

A DHS spokesperson said Sherrill has "consistently shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who've broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than she ever has for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America," while adding it does not comment specifically on matters involving former personnel like Bovino.

Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.

Sherrill had publicly condemned Bovino and Rutgers’ College Republicans for holding the event.

Rutgers is New Jersey’s state university, and the governor appoints some of its board members. Delaware Valley radio host Rich Zeoli said the state gives the New Brunswick school about $1.4 billion annually, adding the argument can be made she is "using a classic intimidation tactic to silence speech she doesn't like."

MARKWAYNE MULLIN GOES OFF ON DEMS’ 'GARBAGE' MEMORIAL DAY ‘POLITICAL STUNT’ AT ICE FACILITY

A file photo shows a Rutgers University campus in New Jersey. Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill criticized the university’s College Republican chapter for hosting retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino in New Brunswick. (Eduardo Munoz/Reuters)

Sherrill urged attendees to press Bovino on why he chooses "cruelty over humanity" and what he thinks of the November election results and the argument that they represent a collective rebuke of his enforcement approach.

The North Carolina native shot back at Sherrill, saying her statement was "spoken like a true lib who puts illegal aliens before her own citizens."

"Gubner, I am deeply disappointed in your penchant for using the Governor’s Office to limit Constitutional rights of Americans," Bovino said in a statement.

"This coming from someone who cheated at the Naval Academy (you weren’t allowed to walk), and enriched yourself via insider trading in defense stocks as a Congressgirl — priceless." Sherrill has said she was barred from walking at the graduation not because she was involved in cheating but because she declined to identify classmates involved.

New Jersey State Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, R-Point Pleasant Beach, said Sherrill’s criticism of Bovino contrasts with her silence over Democrats electing a candidate in the state who was once acquaintances with the mastermind behind the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

"The thought-police strike again," Kanitra said.

"I didn’t see you weighing in when any Adam Hamawy said some pretty heinous things recently? That didn’t seem to warrant a tweet," he said, referring to the Mercer County doctor and former defense trial witness for the Blind Sheikh who won the race to succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-N.J.

Hamawy was never charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Abdel-Rahman, and his campaign previously told Fox News Digital related criticisms amount to "guilt-by-association" shaming and that Republicans and right-wing press are simply concerned that Hamawy will be "Donald Trump's worst nightmare."

Bovino later challenged Sherrill to attend his event, which the governor did not attend.

"Tell you what, come on down to Rutgers and put your insider-trading money where your mouth is. You won’t be able to cheat your way through this one."

Sherrill’s 2025 gubernatorial campaign previously denied the stock-trading allegation raised by Bovino, which stemmed from Republican challenger Jack Ciattarelli’s claim that she "cash[ed] in to the tune of $7 million" by "flipping stocks" while in Congress.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
excerpt:
Masha was in her kitchen when she heard the explosions blast through the city

The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boo...
body_text:
Masha was in her kitchen when she heard the explosions blast through the city

The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.

Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.

Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.

At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.

Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.

Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.

Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.

"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.

But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.

"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."

The Northern Bridge crossing is closed to traffic while emergency response teams work to clear the debris

From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.

Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.

On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.

"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."

The main bridges over the River Dnipro - that cuts through Kyiv - were the target of Russian strikes

That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.

Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.

Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.

To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.

But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.

The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.

"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72

title: Trump seeks nuclear cuts at summit with Putin and Xi, but prospects are low
excerpt: VIENNA — The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China are set to meet in the Chinese tech metropolis of Shenzhen on Thursday in an event that has been hailed as “historic” by all sides. Among the topics ...
body_text:
VIENNA — The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China are set to meet in the Chinese tech metropolis of Shenzhen on Thursday in an event that has been hailed as “historic” by all sides. Among the topics raised for discussion are reductions in global nuclear stockpiles. But experts caution that while the meeting itself is a positive development, any major breakthrough remains unlikely.

Expectations for the get-together ratcheted up over the course of the past week, particularly in Russia, where the event has been ascribed undertones of a “Yalta 2.0,” referencing the 1945 conference that reordered the world after World War II.

From the U.S. side, meanwhile, the Trump administration surprised many observers by pushing for discussions about reducing nuclear weapons while in Shenzhen. The last strategic arms control treaty between Russia and the U.S., in the form of New START, expired in February, leaving the two largest nuclear states without numerical limits on atomic arsenals  for the first time since 1972.

China, meanwhile, was not a party to New START and was, in fact, never part of any strategic arms treaty like it. Beijing is estimated to have the third-largest nuclear arsenal in the world, at several hundred, although analysts believe it has been working to significantly increase this number in recent years. The U.S. and Russia each have stockpiles of around 4,000  nuclear weapons.

This numerical discrepancy is also why China has previously bristled at the idea of discussing strategic arms limitation in a trilateral format like the one U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing in the run-up to the meeting. Although Beijing has confirmed the meeting, it has stopped short of officially saying strategic arms dialogue would be on the agenda. “The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations,” said Mao Ning, spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

This avoids naming explicitly what the U.S. has asked for. “The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters last Friday.

Nikita Degtyarev, research coordinator at the Vienna-based Open Nuclear Network, an international NGO dealing with nuclear arms control, said he was realistic about achievable outcomes.

“I don’t have very high expectations, but I’m happy that it’s happening,” he said in an interview. “A meeting at the leader level is something else than the ongoing P5 dialogue and other existing formats.”

The P5 dialogue brings together the five Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty-recognized nuclear weapons states – the U.S., Russia, China, France and the U.K. – on a working level to discuss nuclear policy and risk reduction.

“If there is any outcome of the trilateral meeting relating to nuclear issues, it will likely be more of a political statement than a verifiable and restrictive arms control agreement,” said Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues and senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank CSIS,

“I think the most likely significant outcome would be a reiteration of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” Degtyarev said. A more substantive or groundbreaking agreement was also unlikely because there simply wasn’t enough time for lower-level officials to hammer out the details of any possible agreement that the leaders could sign, he said.

Major arms control treaties often take years of meticulous crafting at the working level before heads of state come together to sign them.

Trump first raised the topic of denuclearization in the context of the summit to reporters on Oct. 19, a day after the Wall Street Journal first reported about a proposed trilateral meeting.

A possible wildcard agenda item remains in the form of artificial intelligence in nuclear weapons. AI in nuclear command and control has emerged as a somewhat more promising topic and a potential area for agreement more palatable to all sides than commitments to numerical reductions or verification mechanisms.

The South China Morning Post reported Nov. 11, citing sources familiar with preparations, that working-level teams had discussed AI in critical weapons systems and that the agenda was shifting toward potential common ground, particularly AI’s role in nuclear command and control. One source characterized AI governance of nuclear weapons as an “easy deliverable” consistent with past policies.

This “could give Trump something to announce without requiring anyone to compromise their nuclear posture,” Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told the French press agency AFP.

Under the previous U.S. administration, Biden and Xi reaffirmed the importance of human decision-making in nuclear command and control in November 2024, while Russia has so far resisted such language, including in the P5 process.

Much may depend on the willingness of Beijing to engage in strategic arms dialogue, which has indicated it has no major desire to discuss this topic while China remains a numerical underdog in the quantity of its warheads.

“China is the host and will probably closely stage-manage the event and the agenda,” Degtyarev said. Xi Jinping’s style of international engagements tends to be highly scripted and predictable, at odds with Trump’s more improvisational approach.

The common denominator for all three leaders is more likely to be good publicity. “Trump is probably genuine about his interest in nuclear arms reduction,” Degtyarev assessed, “but probably also from a self-serving and PR point of view.”

Though the meeting is historic in nature for its assembling of a triumvirate of the world’s most powerful men, “the Yalta 2.0 comparisons are overblown,” said Degtyarev. “The scale of the historical moment is simply different.”

Linus Höller is Defense News’ Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

title: Pentagon fails ninth straight audit despite progress in organizing finances
excerpt:
The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report released Monday, but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.
...
body_text:
The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report released Monday, but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.

Defense Department CFO Jules Hurst told Reuters an independent auditor found that financial statements for 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 standalone reporting entities passed in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, up from 11 the prior year. Those entities account for 56% of the department’s assets and 86% of its liabilities.

“For the first time ever, a majority of assets from the department are on clean opinions,” Hurst said. The audits check whether financial statements are fairly presented and whether financial systems and processes are sound.

The Pentagon is a vast bureaucracy that has struggled with some 149 financial management systems, many of which are inadequate and outdated. They include technology built on 50-year-old computer code.

As the administration seeks a record $1.5 trillion in national defense spending from Congress, modernizing those systems has become a priority as the Pentagon strives to show lawmakers it can be trusted.

The Pentagon as a whole was first audited in 2018 and has consistently ​failed to pass annual audits because of its ⁠system and accounting problems. Congress gave it 10 years to pass, which falls in the fiscal year starting in October 2027.

Among the entities passing an audit for the first time in fiscal 2026 was the Pentagon’s Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund.

To complete an audit without relying on the antiquated systems, officials drew from 61 core systems in the Pentagon’s more modern cloud-based War Data Platform. They obtained statistically significant data samples that were used for the audit.

The department is also using artificial intelligence tools from Palantir and xAI, alongside in-house applications, to automate financial reconciliations and documentation.

“Passing the audit is ultimately a time problem,” Hurst said, saying AI allows auditors to test more data.

Beginning this year, the Pentagon plans to consolidate 25 separate audit opinions into eight, ahead of seeking a full department-wide opinion in fiscal 2028.

Congress phased in audit requirements for federal agencies over decades, and most major agencies must have their financial statements audited annually.

title: New pact positions the Philippines as a defense hub for Australian troops
excerpt: MANILA, Philippines — Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian inve...
body_text:
MANILA, Philippines — Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.

The Nov. 15 Defense Cooperation Agreement, or DCA, is designed to cut administrative bottlenecks and create a more efficient coordination system to fast-track bilateral defense activities.

So far the two countries’ military exchanges have largely fallen under a 1995 memorandum of agreement, while troop exchanges were guided by the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, signed in 2007 and effective since 2012.

According to Australia’s Department of Defence, the new pact covers intelligence-sharing, military training, the transfer of aerial and surface drones, maritime activities, and military infrastructure.

“This new Defence Cooperation Arrangement will deepen practical cooperation between our defense forces and create new opportunities to work together in support of regional security,” Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in a statement.

Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the new DCA reduces bureaucratic barriers, particularly in troop deployment, and would allow Australia to rapidly deploy troops to aid in Philippine disaster response.

“Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10 … and it will be more purposeful and not ad hoc,” Teodoro told reporters following the signing.

The move comes as Australia recalibrates its defense posture in response to China’s expanding military capabilities, growing missile reach, and increasing use of gray-zone tactics and economic coercion in the Indo-Pacific.

“From Australia’s point of view, the Philippines is our first line of defense,” Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior fellow Euan Graham told Defense News.

Australia has experienced harassment by PLA forces, including dangerous maritime maneuvers, laser targeting in its northern exclusive economic zone, and the use of sonar and flares in close proximity to Royal Australian Navy vessels.

Like Australia, the Philippines faces Chinese pressure head-on. Chinese ships have used high-powered water cannons, pointed military-grade lasers, rammed, and attacked Armed Forces of the Philippines vessels and personnel.

When asked if the DCA was meant to boost deterrence in the Taiwan Strait, Teodoro emphasized the agreement will bolster “deterrence in the West Philippine Sea” and in “Philippine territory.”

Australia marked a historic peacetime shift toward a strategy of denial in 2023, most recently codified in the 2026 national defense strategy.

The idea is to reshape the Australian Defense Force into an integrated, focused military capable of deterring and denying access to its northern approaches, which includes deploying a forward-defense force.

Earlier this year, Australia created the new Littoral Maneuver Group under the 18th Sustainment Brigade headquartered in Brisbane, to operate farther north, making the Philippines an important part of that strategy.

But Australia can only deploy small units, analyst Graham cautioned. And keeping these mobile forces supplied and operational in archipelagic countries like the Philippines is challenging, as troops and equipment are moved across widely dispersed islands during operations.

To that end, the new cooperation agreement is expected to facilitate discussions on potential Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.

A list of five Luzon bases slated to receive funding for eight infrastructure projects was expected to be finalized around August this year. However, only one base has been discussed in detail so far, officials told Defense News.

Teodoro previously clarified that base agreements with Australia will follow a different model than the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between the Philippines and the United States, which includes provisions for prepositioning military equipment and assets.

The Australian “basing” arrangements, officials said, would include areas that are not traditional bases.

Rather than a large basing presence, what the Australian military needs is access to locations that could sustain its forces during operations and contingencies.

Discussions so far have included sustainment and logistics to support joint operations while troops spread across the archipelago’s most complex, most challenging, and remote terrains.

Graham said Australia’s role in the Philippines is distinct but complementary to that of the United States. While physical locations could overlap, the infrastructure projects would be different.

Canberra and Manila in 2021 signed the Mutual Support Logistics Arrangement, which covers fuel and other supplies for aircraft and vessels, transportation, logistics, and coordination.

“The importance of logistics can’t be underestimated. It’s not just about getting your fighting force fighting. You’ve got to supply them with food, fuel, and ammunition during all of that,” Graham said.

With the new DCA with Australia in place, joint exercises, especially Exercise ALON, will see a larger iteration next year, Teodoro said.

Exercise ALON, first held in 2023, is the biennial flagship joint training exercise between countries, focused on amphibious operations.

The 2025 edition saw Australia’s largest overseas military exercise for the year and showcased the ADF projecting combat forces into the contested West Philippine Sea, Graham said.

Apart from maritime training, Teodoro said there will be more aerial, land, cyber, and multidomain training exercises between Filipino and Australian troops.

Military officials told Defense News that Army training has been a priority area for the Australian military’s training playbook in the Philippines. The focus follows sweeping changes in both countries’ land forces to prepare them for modern conflicts.

While the Philippine Army expands from its signature jungle and urban warfare expertise toward coastal defense, the Australian ground service has pivoted toward littoral warfare.

Since 2023, exchanges have focused on techniques, tactics, and procedures for amphibious operations, Army spokesperson Col. Louie Dema-ala told Defense News.

But future iterations will include advanced training, Dema-ala said. “We are transitioning into a multi-domain capable Army.”

The exchange is not one-sided. Australia also stands to benefit from the Philippine Army’s experience operating in dense jungle terrain.

“This is not just a one-way process. We can learn from the jungle warfare fighting skills, and I think that’s important to stress. No one can tell us about the Philippines better than the Filipinos,” Graham said.

Leilani Chavez is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. Her reporting expertise is in East Asian politics, development projects, environmental issues and security.

title: Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House
excerpt: On the eve of Democratic leadership elections in the United States House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries has confirmed plans to force fellow Democrats to take a recorded vote on his nomination for...
body_text:
On the eve of Democratic leadership elections in the United States House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries has confirmed plans to force fellow Democrats to take a recorded vote on his nomination for speaker.

Jeffries, the chamber’s current minority leader, told reporters at the US Capitol on Tuesday he was taking the new approach instead of — as some of his top allies had hoped — a vote by acclamation, which requires no ballot.

The move effectively forces House Democrats to publicly weigh in on whether they support Jeffries’s leadership.

Jeffries, a New York Democrat poised to become the House’s first Black speaker, argued that a recorded vote was the same method his party used when it retook control of the chamber in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term.

“It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in, one way or the other, on who the caucus feels is best positioned … to help move us forward into the new Congress,” Jeffries said during his news conference.

The strategy shift, which was first reported by Punchbowl News, comes amid growing Democratic dissent over having Jeffries in control of the party’s messaging and policy priorities in the US House.

Some progressive members, particularly newly elected ones, had reportedly threatened to call for a recorded vote to extract policy concessions from Jeffries.

Without unanimous backing, the vote to nominate Jeffries could highlight dissent within the Democratic Party.

One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, has publicly refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.

“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.

Jeffries’s preemptive countermove effectively strips progressive members of leverage heading into Wednesday’s closed-door vote by forcing them to go on record against his leadership.

It also highlights a weakness in their efforts: the lack of another candidate for speaker.

On Monday, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts dismissed the idea she would mount a challenge to Jeffries.

Last week, she rallied her social media followers to sign a petition to shape the Democratic majority’s agenda, spurring questions about whether she would run for the speaker role. But she has since brushed those aside.

“I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people,” Pressley said at a town hall in her district.

When asked about the resistance he faces from his fellow Democrats, Jeffries told reporters they would “have to talk to” dissenting party members about why they oppose his leadership.

“We’re going to have a vote tomorrow. The caucus is going to be able to work its will. And we’ll see what the outcome is tomorrow,” Jeffries said. “In less than 24 hours, you’ll be able to know.”

Jeffries is expected to handily win Wednesday’s vote, which would give the leader an idea of the support he has when the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The speakership will be confirmed in a separate roll call vote on the floor of the US House early in the new year.

title: NSA claims temporary internal network outage caused by ‘scheduled routine maintenance’ – live
excerpt:
Sources told CNN there was no evidence of cyberattack against NSA Net, the network that allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally

Hello and welcome to the US politics li...
body_text:
Sources told CNN there was no evidence of cyberattack against NSA Net, the network that allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

The final Senate race of this year’s midterm elections could be resolved tomorrow if Alaska election officials run the state’s ranked choice voting system to determine the result.

With 98% of ballots counted, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is out in front with 49.98% of the vote. By contrast, incumbent Republican senator Dan S Sullivan has a 45.93% share, according to the latest Associated Press figures.

In terms of actual voting numbers, Peltola is ahead by just over 11,000, with 141,637 compared to Sullivan’s 130,162. All eyes will be on Peltola to see if she can keep the pace to achieve 50% of the ballot, two weeks on from the election.

If not, then voters’ second choice votes will be counted. The outcome will determine the final balance of power in the chamber for the next two years, with Democrats already holding a 55-44 majority.

It comes in a turbulent Alaska race, which has seen president Trump demand that Peltola be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Piling on, Alaska’s Republican governor has since ordered an investigation into Peltola’s campaign.

A New York Times investigation reported that operatives working with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit another Dan Sullivan – Dan J Sullivan – a retired teacher from Petersburg, to split the incumbent’s vote. Peltola and her campaign have denied this.

The ‘other’ Sullivan, who stood as an independent candidate, has only received 4,684 votes – a 1.65% share – and is looking unlikely to be the cause of the Republican senator’s failure should he not retain his seat.

Elsewhere, president Trump has arrived in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, where he is due to meet south east Asian leaders and take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

Donald Trump defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after treasury secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that he has been pushing “for months” to add Megaspeed, the data center company led by an alleged Chinese spy who was reportedly in a relationship with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, to the US trade blacklist.

Trump blasted the new leadership of CBS News’ 60 Minutes, which was overhauled under the network’s conservative editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. In a social media post, the president was particularly critical of a report on the more than 800 American service members wounded and 23 killed in the war in Iran that 60 Minutes aired on Sunday.

⁠Trump also said that he ⁠would ​“not ‌mind” ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia. The president says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denied that national security has been put at risk.

The president also continued to shift responsibility to the Biden administration for the nationwide ground stop over the weekend. Trump said that he needed more funding to overhaul the outdated telecommunication system responsible for the disruptions.

The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren, the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, that she could face “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump. The warning mirrors other letters justice department officials have sent to Democratic lawmakers who have indicated they will investigate the Trump administration when the party becomes the majority in Congress next year.

A federal appeals court heard arguments in Donald Trump’s hush money case, as the president tries to see the case shifted to federal court where he could have it dismissed on grounds of immunity. The hearing concerned a May 2024 ruling that found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.

The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.

“Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization. “The endemic measles transmission has now been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and United States.” Silva made the final decision on US elimination status.

Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. The measles vaccine is safe and highly effective. However, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the US following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation.

The nation’s largest doctors group, the American Medical Association, described loss of measles elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback for our nation”.

The loss of measles-free status comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, spent nearly two years sowing confusion about the safety of vaccines. In just one recent example, Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, arguing without evidence that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.

“As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families,” said Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic senator-elect. “Nothing makes that clearer than the loss of our measles elimination status.” The loss of elimination status has already heightened criticism of Kennedy. High-profile epidemiologists called Kennedy’s work at the health department “malpractice” and equivalent to a “crime scene”.

A reminder that the NSA’s temporary network failure today is the latest in a string of tech outages in the last week that have affected the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft, Chase Bank and JP Morgan.

The outage of a highly classified internal network at the National Security Agency (NSA), was the result of “scheduled routine maintenance,” an NSA spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

As I noted earlier, following a CNN report, the NSA Net, the network that allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally, was down. However, sources told CNN that there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

During his confirmation hearing today, Hung Cao said the eight suicide attempts on board the USS Abraham Lincoln – which returned last month from a record-breaking deployment riddled with mental health crises and concerns about living conditions on the warship – were actually “suicide mitigations”.

Cao, who is hoping to become the permanent secretary of the US Navy, defended the situation on board during the 264 consecutive days at sea.

“The mental health issues you see as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicides mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists,” Cao said while fielding questions from Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat. “Normally, most carrier strike groups, when they deploy, have about one to two suicides … We had zero actual suicides on board the Abraham Lincoln.”

Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday, after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.

The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him.

In a new memoir, Joe Biden offers harsh criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has led Ukraine through four-and-a-half years of war against Russia. According to Biden, the Ukrainian president was “difficult to work with”, “moody and stubborn in our private conversations”, and “not as grateful as I expected” for US diplomatic support and military aid.

Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, was published on Tuesday, shortly before his 84th birthday and as he battles advanced prostate cancer. Largely a trumpeting of achievements in office, with scant admission of failings ultimately crowned by his own party deeming him unfit for office and forcing his withdrawal from the 2024 campaign against Donald Trump, the book has not been well reviewed.

The war in Ukraine takes up much of the middle of the book. Detailing frustrating talks with Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, Biden describes the buildup to war and US-Ukraine co-operation from the invasion of February 2022 until Biden left office in January 2025.

His portrait of Zelenskyy is not entirely negative.

“I had worried that President Zelenskyy, who had come from such an unlikely background [as a comedian and actor] might not have the right stuff for a crisis like this one,” Biden writes. “This was no TV comedy.” But, the former president adds, he found himself impressed by Zelenskyy’s fortitude, and “delighted that my worries proved to be unfounded”.

At a press conference earlier, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, pledged to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, restore Medicaid cuts, expand Medicare eligibility, end “the reckless and costly war of choice” on Iran, end tariffs, and end Citizens United.

“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he said.

He also called for banning members of Congress from trading stocks, saying: “That will be a high priority. This is what the American people are demanding that we do, and we are going to execute on that mission.”

Jeffries was speaking ahead of the vote tomorrow to elect the next House speaker, which he is expected to win. Asked about progressive resistance to making him speaker, Jeffries replied: “You’ll have to ask, you know, those individuals that you believe are resistant to voting for me in caucus tomorrow.”

The blue wave has hit Washington, and with the flood of new Democratic lawmakers comes a debate over who should lead the party. Yesterday, Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen said his campaign to unseat Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader is gathering momentum. He has painted himself as the underdog candidate to Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade. What does this leadership battle tell us about the kind of party Democrats want to be?

In today’s episode of our Stateside podcast, Kai Wright speaks to the Guardian’s senior politics reporter Chris Stein about Van Hollen’s chances, and hears from the Guardian’s midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang about why new senators in her region are having doubts about Schumer.

Lawmakers in the Senate health, labor and pensions committee are set to vote on Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Wednesday. A reminder that the FDA is the body that oversees US approvals for prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs and vaccines, as well as much of the country’s food supply.

Overton has received bipartisan pushback to head up the agency, which sits within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). During a confirmation hearing in September, she faced questions from Republican and Democratic lawmakers about her stance on vaccines. While she said that “every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective”, Overton gave evasive answers about how she would push back against Donald Trump and his administration when they undermine trust in vaccines at a time when the US is experiencing the highest number of measles cases in decades (the US has since lost its measles elimination status).

Overton also did not correct the president’s statement that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) could be “quite lethal” during an executive order announcement about revisions to the childhood vaccine schedule. This despite the scientific consensus that inoculation is the best method of prevention for all three viruses.

At the time, Senator Bill Cassidy, the health committee’s Republican chair, said Overton’s “active role” in the directive was “almost disqualifying”.

On Sunday, Cassidy told CBS News that he remained uncertain about Overton’s path to confirmation. “I still have questions. And so, I cannot tell you the outcome of that vote right now,” the outgoing senator said.

“We’re not going to have perfection,” Cassidy added. “The question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody’s mind but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence,”

If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A former physician, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term.

Hung Cao, who currently serves as the acting Navy secretary, is facing lawmakers on the Senate armed services committee to be confirmed as the permanent top official.

However, in order to be confirmed Cao will need 60 votes for a congressional waiver to exempt him from the federal law that requires former military officers to have been retired from active-duty service for at least seven years before they are eligible to take top civilian Pentagon positions.

Since Cao only retired as a Navy captain in 2021, he’ll need at least seven Democrats to cross the aisle and confirm him, compared to the usual simple majority required for a presidential nomination.

Jensen Huang, the embattled former CEO of Nvidia, will appear before House lawmakers on the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews on 1 December.

Huang will appear alongside Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the Republican chairs of the respective committees. Huang’s testimony will come after he resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia last week following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Her company, Megaspeed, was under investigation for purchasing Nvidia’s advanced chips and allegedly diverting them to China.

While the battle between Democrats Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer continues for Senate majority leader in the new Congress, in the House Hakeem Jeffries is still poised to clinch role of Speaker, making history as the first Black member to lead the lower chamber.

As of now, there doesn’t seem to be any clear opposition to Jeffries’ bid. Last week, the long-serving Democratic congressman Glenn Ivey told me on the phone that Jeffries is “a shoo-in”.

“I don’t even know if he’ll have any competition. It could well be done by acclamation [voice vote]. I guess we’ll just have to see,” he added.

Today, however, Punchbowl News reported that Jeffries instead plans to ask for a recorded vote in the Democratic caucus meeting on Wednesday, as a sign that he is not worried about the numbers he has to win.
 
 
 A reminder that while the election for Senate leadership happens in a closed-door, secret ballot, the House Speaker is elected by the entire chamber in the new year. As of now, Democrats have an 85-seat majority in the House, with 18 races yet to be called.

The highly classified network that the national security agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to a report by CNN, citing six people familiar with the matter.

NSA Net, the network, allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally. According to CNN’s sources, there is no evidence of a cyber-attack, but the NSA has now launched staggered arrivals of their staff.

The Guardian has contacted the NSA for comment.

In lighter news today, new members in the US House are all taking part in the time honored tradition of the suite selection lottery, where every incoming representative has the chance to snag one of the available offices for the new Congress.

title: Using law to try to silence abuse victims is ‘ultimate form of gaslighting’, MPs told
excerpt:
Woman sued by alleged rapist tells justice committee that Slapp lawsuits present perpetrator as victim of wrongdoing

Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to silence their...
body_text:
Woman sued by alleged rapist tells justice committee that Slapp lawsuits present perpetrator as victim of wrongdoing

Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to silence their victims using the law are “the ultimate form of gaslighting”, MPs have heard.

Verity Nevitt, a co-founder of the Gemini Project, a survivor-led nonprofit organisation, told the House of Commons justice committee about the ordeal of being sued by the man she and her sister, Lucy, respectively accused of sexual abuse and rape.

At Tuesday’s session, held after the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault and the allegations of improper behaviour against David Walliams, which he denies, MPs heard that wealthy and powerful men silenced victims through injunctions, non-disclosure agreements and strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps. The latter are used to harass or intimidate opponents speaking out on matters of public interest.

Nevitt said: “When you experience rape or sexual assault, choice is taken from you, and being subject to a Slapp replicates those dynamics in the sense that you have no choice but to be subject to it … And I think that also means that these cases are quite attractive to someone who is coercive, controlling.

“I think Slapps allow a flipping of the script where the perpetrator is presented as a victim of wrongdoing, and then the victim survivor is presented as the aggressor by being made a defendant. It’s an egregious reversal of reality, and it’s the ultimate form of gaslighting.”

Nevitt and her sister reported the man to police but, when the case was dropped, they decided to name him on social media to warn others, which led to him suing them.

They eventually reached an out-of-court agreement and, having waived their right to anonymity, the sisters could talk about the case without naming him.

Nevitt told MPs that in the case brought against her and her sister the truth “didn’t matter at all” – it was all about the costs. She said that after the first hearing, the solicitor took the sisters aside and told them they would have to find £100,000 to make it to the next hearing.

Jennifer Robinson, a barrister and co-author of Silenced Women: Why The Law Fails Women and How to Fight Back, told MPs that survivors who were sued faced huge costs. “The chilling effect is actually much broader than simply women themselves who want to speak out,” she said. “It’s also having a chilling effect on journalists’ willingness and their newspapers’ willingness to report their stories, which is not in the public interest. We can’t tackle violence against women if we can’t talk about it.”

Harriet Wistrich, the chief executive of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said there was a good argument for “very severe cost capping” in such cases.

Rupert Cowper-Coles, a partner and head of media at RPC solicitors, told the committee the UK was a “major outlier amongst western democracies” because it did not have a general anti-Slapp law but one that only covered disclosures relating to economic crime.

Robinson said: “Why are we privileging the protection of public interest speech on economic crimes and not for crimes against women in the context of the crisis of violence against women that we have in society?”

title: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
excerpt:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry is cited as saying by state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a ...
body_text:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry is cited as saying by state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

A technical malfunction is preliminarily believed to be the cause of Tuesday's crash, the ministry added. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.

Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.

title: LaNeve formally nominated for Army chief of staff role
excerpt: The Trump administration nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve as chief of staff of the Army, according to a Monday congressional notice, moving formally to fill the role left vacant after Defense Secreta...
body_text:
The Trump administration nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve as chief of staff of the Army, according to a Monday congressional notice, moving formally to fill the role left vacant after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April.

LaNeve, also the Army’s vice chief of staff, has been serving as the acting chief of staff in the interim. He needs Senate confirmation to officially take the position.

“He is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield. I cannot think of anyone better to serve as our next Chief of Staff of the Army,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a social media statement regarding LaNeve’s nomination. Telle said he anticipated “working with the Senate” to get LaNeve — and Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans, who would take on vice chief responsibilities — confirmed.

The administration nominated Evans to fill the role of vice chief of staff of the Army, according to another Monday congressional notice.

After former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned in September amid reported tension with Hegseth, the Army has been without Senate-confirmed top uniformed and civilian leadership. Telle has not been officially nominated to fill the Army secretary role.

LaNeve, who formerly served as Hegseth’s military aide, was nominated for the vice chief role before former Vice Chief James Mingus had completed the typical four-year term in the position. Hegseth’s tenure in the Pentagon has been marked by senior leadership shakeups and the firing of over a dozen generals and admirals.

LaNeve has drawn congressional ire for eliminating the 600-member “Unmanned Assault Battalion,” which was created as part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade. He has since sought to reassure industry leaders that the Army is committed to autonomy, changing the name of the command charged with shaping the future force to U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

Evans is currently serving as director of Army staff in Washington, according to the service. Previously, he was special assistant to the commanding general at Fort Shafter, Hawaii. He also worked as the special operations command chief of staff from 2021 to 2023, and commanded the Special Operations Joint Task Force-Afghanistan from 2020 to 2021.

He was promoted lieutenant general in September of last year and major general in February 2022.

The nominations come after massive Republican losses during midterm elections, which will shift control of the House and Senate to Democrats during the next year’s congressional session.

Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

Who are the Neets? UK youth jo...
