Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.

The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a “watershed moment” for young people.

But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government.

In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage.

“A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government: employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.”

Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups.

“The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said.

Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work.

He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”.

Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.

It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.

The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim.

People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.

The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.

Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.

The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office.

Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.

Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”

But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts.

McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”

On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate.

And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences. I believe this is likely to be the case.”

Business leaders welcomed the recommendations, in particular the call to backtrack on Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions with a tax cut for under-25s, starting in retail and hospitality.

Maxine Bligh, the interim chief executive of the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, said: “Tackling the Neet [not in education, employment or training] crisis gives ministers the perfect opportunity to reconsider a guaranteed hours gamble that risks costing jobs and damaging the chances of young people accessing the labour market.”

Industry chiefs have intensified their lobbying against the government’s Employment Rights Act, with bosses finding a warm reception from Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Labour was pressing ahead with an “unemployment act” that would hit youth jobs. “You cannot solve a youth jobs emergency without jobs, and this government has spent two years destroying them.”

Government analysis published this year showed estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.

But unions and charities urged Burnham not to water down the plans, arguing that low-paid and insecure work had contributed significantly to Britain’s youth jobs crisis.

Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, said “crucial policies” on workers’ rights needed to be retained. “We are clear that the government must ensure that employment is fairly paid and secure, with workers being treated with dignity and respect.”

Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto. Under Starmer, however, elements of the party’s plan to “make work pay” were watered down amid opposition from business.

Clare McNeil, the chief executive of the charity Timewise, said: “Where we disagree with Alan Milburn is in any suggestion that the new responsibilities in the Employment Rights Bill will stop employers hiring.”

Allies of the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, who had championed the government’s zero-hours plan as Starmer’s deputy, insisted that her proposals would not discourage employers from hiring young people. However, she is no longer in charge of the policy, which must now be implemented by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.

title: States put speed-limiting devices in reckless drivers' cars
excerpt:
A LifeSafer GPS-powered speed limiter displays a 35 mph limit and helps prevent the driver from accelerating beyond the posted speed limit. (LifeSafer ISA)

We've all seen it. You're driving down the ...
body_text:
A LifeSafer GPS-powered speed limiter displays a 35 mph limit and helps prevent the driver from accelerating beyond the posted speed limit. (LifeSafer ISA)

We've all seen it. You're driving down the highway when someone flies past you at a ridiculous speed. Maybe they're weaving through traffic while everyone else tries to stay out of their way. Now, states are turning to speed-limiting devices that could stop some of the most dangerous drivers from doing it again.

Virginia has already started installing GPS-powered devices in vehicles used by certain reckless-driving offenders. Washington, D.C., has a similar program, and more jurisdictions are exploring the technology. The idea sounds promising. Instead of simply telling someone to slow down, the device can actually restrict how fast their car accelerates.

However, there's a catch. Some drivers using these systems have reported GPS glitches that mistakenly apply the speed limits of nearby roads. And that raises a question worth asking. What happens when your car refuses to accelerate because its GPS thinks you're somewhere else?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH

The technology is called Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA). It uses GPS location information and digital maps to determine the posted speed limit. Here's how it works. Let's say you're traveling on a road with a 45 mph speed limit. As your vehicle reaches 45 mph, the device restricts additional acceleration. Pressing harder on the gas pedal won't normally make the car accelerate beyond that limit.

However, the system doesn't automatically slam on the brakes or shut off the engine. Instead, it limits the vehicle's ability to accelerate. That means a vehicle traveling downhill could still exceed the posted limit because of gravity.

Some systems also allow brief overrides when additional acceleration is necessary for safety. Think of it as a speed governor that automatically adjusts as you move between roads. The important difference comes down to control. Many newer vehicles already recognize speed limits and warn drivers when they're going too fast. These aftermarket devices take things further by restricting acceleration.

Virginia launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on July 1. The state allows courts to require speed-limiting technology for certain driving offenses, including reckless driving and racing. The Virginia DMV can also require participation in qualifying cases involving excessive demerit points. For eligible drivers, the program offers a way to maintain restricted driving privileges rather than face a full license suspension. According to a Nov. 2 report, approximately 100 devices had been installed in Virginia since July. Many participants faced reckless-driving charges or convictions. Some cases involved speeds exceeding 100 mph.

The restrictions are serious. Qualifying drivers may need the equipment installed in every vehicle they own or co-own. They must also comply with restrictions on which vehicles they can operate. Then there's the cost. Participants generally pay installation and ongoing service fees, although financial assistance may be available for those who qualify. The goal is to let certain drivers continue essential travel while reducing the risk of dangerous speeding.

Virginia has company in exploring this approach. Washington, D.C. launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on Oct. 1, 2025. Under the program, D.C. driver's license holders convicted of aggravated reckless driving must enroll and operate only authorized vehicles equipped with the technology.

Washington state passed legislation in 2025 requiring speed-limiting devices in certain cases involving dangerous speeding and driving restrictions. However, those requirements won't take effect until Jan. 1, 2029. Meanwhile, New York City is considering a proposal introduced on Oct. 22. It would require vehicle owners who accumulate 16 school-zone speeding violations within 12 months to install speed-limiting devices. The New York City proposal remains in committee and has not become law. These programs differ in scope. Still, they show how policymakers are increasingly considering technology as a response to dangerous driving.

JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT

LifeSafer's Intelligent Speed Assistance device uses GPS and digital maps to identify speed limits and restrict vehicle acceleration. (LifeSafer ISA)

GPS technology is incredibly useful. But anyone who's followed navigation directions onto the wrong road knows it can make mistakes. Consider this situation. You're driving on a highway with a 65 mph speed limit. A service road running alongside it has a 35 mph limit. If your GPS mistakenly places you on the service road, the speed limiter could apply the lower limit. Your vehicle wouldn't suddenly brake, but it could restrict additional acceleration even though you're traveling on a highway with a higher speed limit. That's the type of GPS problem some Virginia participants have reported.

Early users reportedly experienced situations where their devices applied lower limits from nearby roads. Officials acknowledged the complaints and said they were working on fixes. To be clear, the reports establish that location errors have occurred. They do not establish a pattern of crashes caused by those errors. That could become a safety concern when a driver needs additional acceleration to merge into traffic, but the vehicle won't respond as expected. That's a potential safety concern officials need to address before these systems become more widespread.

Some systems provide temporary overrides when drivers need additional acceleration. Virginia's proposed technical standards outline specific limits for emergency overrides, although those requirements have not yet been finalized. Under the proposal, an override would last no longer than 30 seconds, permit a maximum of 5 mph above the posted speed limit and allow no more than two overrides per driving cycle.

Those specifications appear in regulations published Oct. 19. The rules remain proposed, with public comments accepted through Dec. 18. The limits are intended to balance safety with the program's goal of preventing excessive speeding. However, they also show that an emergency override may provide much less acceleration than a driver expects. That's why clear instructions and reliable operation are so important.

There's a serious reason states are considering these devices. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 11,288 people died in speeding-related traffic crashes in 2024. Speeding contributed to 29% of all U.S. traffic fatalities that year. Those numbers help explain why officials want something more effective than another speeding ticket.

A driver who repeatedly ignores speed limits may continue taking risks after paying fines. And suspending someone's license doesn't physically prevent that person from getting behind the wheel. Speed-limiting technology offers another option. A properly functioning device can prevent certain excessive speeds while allowing qualifying drivers to continue traveling to work or handling essential responsibilities.

However, speed limits tell only part of the safety story. Someone can drive recklessly without exceeding the posted limit. Following too closely can still cause a crash. Bad weather can also make a legally permitted speed dangerous. So, these devices may help reduce extreme speeding, but they cannot guarantee safe driving.

NEW BIG RIG SAFETY TECH COULD SAVE YOUR LIFE

A driver operates a vehicle equipped with a LifeSafer speed limiter showing a 30 mph speed limit and a current speed of 29 mph. (LifeSafer ISA)

That's the bigger question. For now, these enforcement programs focus on drivers who meet specific legal criteria. There is no nationwide requirement forcing every U.S. driver to install one of these aftermarket speed-limiting devices. However, many newer vehicles already offer speed-limit recognition and warnings. That means some of the technology has become familiar to drivers.

The bigger step involves allowing software to actively restrict acceleration. As more jurisdictions test these programs, lawmakers could consider expanding eligibility. But any expansion would require additional policy decisions. And public acceptance could become a major obstacle. After all, there's a big difference between your dashboard warning you that you're speeding and your car preventing you from accelerating.

There's another issue I think deserves more attention. What happens to all the driving information these systems collect? GPS-based speed limiters need location data to determine which speed limit applies. Depending on the program, they may also record speeding events and other information used to monitor compliance.

Virginia's proposed regulations would require service providers to report certain vehicle events and speed violations, including GPS locations. The proposal also contains a significant additional requirement. Beginning July 1, 2027, new installations would need cameras capable of photographing the driver's seat when the device records a speeding event, if the proposed rules take effect as written.

That raises questions about who can access the information and how long it remains stored. We explored similar privacy concerns in our article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance tracking programs serve a different purpose. However, both technologies show how much information connected vehicles can generate about the people driving them. And once that information exists, clear rules about its collection and use become especially important.

I understand why states want to take this approach. We've all shared the road with someone driving so recklessly that you wonder how they still have a license. And if technology can prevent someone from driving 100 mph through traffic, I see the appeal. What concerns me is putting that much authority in the hands of a GPS system that can make mistakes. I've seen enough technology glitches over the years to know that even sophisticated systems sometimes get things wrong. That's inconvenient when your phone sends you to the wrong address. It's a much bigger concern when you're behind the wheel. I also think states need to be careful about how they expand these programs. Targeting repeat dangerous drivers makes sense. Requiring everyone to surrender control of their vehicle would raise a very different set of questions. Before we go further, I'd like to see stronger evidence that these devices reduce crashes without creating new safety problems. Because ultimately, the goal should be safer roads. And that means making sure the technology earns our trust before we depend on it.

Would you feel safer knowing reckless drivers have speed limiters in their cars, or does the idea of a GPS system controlling your accelerator worry you even more? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

Got a tech question? Get Kurt’s free CyberGuy Newsletter, share your voice, a story idea or comment at CyberGuy.com.

title: Warren grills Trump Navy secretary on cost of Iran war: 'You don't have any idea?'
excerpt:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you kn...
body_text:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.

Warren repeatedly pressed Cao on how much U.S. taxpayers were spending to support the U.S. Navy's blockade on Iranian ports as well as recovering from damage sustained in the conflict. Cao dodged multiple questions, stating that assessments were ongoing or he simply didn't have access to the data.

"Acting Secretary Cao what is the daily cost of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports?" Warren asked.

TRUMP'S $88B IRAN WAR BILL COLLIDES WITH SENATE OPPOSITION

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, speaks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, Jan. 14, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Senator, I do not know the daily cost, ma'am," Cao responded.

"You don't have any idea. You've been running this thing since April and you don't have any idea what that costs," Warren pressed.

IRAN WAR'S PRICE TAG HITS $80B — MORE THAN DOUBLE WHAT CONGRESS WAS TOLD

"Well, sir, I know the rough cost of how much it's costing us so far. But again, the cost of losing the strait–," Cao said.

Warren cut him off, "I'm not asking you that. I just want to have the dollars here. Independent estimates are about $32.5 million a day. Does that sound about right to you?"

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao testifies during the Senate Armed Services Committee hearing titled "The Posture of the Department of the Navy in review of the Defense Authorization Request for FY2027 and the Future Years Defense Program," in Dirksen building on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

BLOCKADE 101: AMERICAN SEA POWER ON DISPLAY AS TRUMP CORNERS IRAN AND WARNS OFF CHINA

"Senator, let me do some quick Asian math in my head. But yes, it's about $30 billion so far," he confirmed.

"So you you confirm that number, and that means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade," she said.

RO KHANNA PITCHES $1,700 CHECKS FOR AMERICANS TO OFFSET IRAN WAR COSTS: 'A CHANCE TO DELIVER'

Warren then moved on to the Iranian attack on the U.S. Navy's base in Bahrain, but Cao once again said he did not know the cost, saying the assessment is still ongoing.

The Senator referenced an estimate from the Wall Street Journal placing the cost at roughly $400 million. When asked if it was accurate, Cao said simply, "I'll find out."

COST OF IRAN WAR EXPLODES AS TOLL ON US AIR FLEET NEARLY DOUBLES

The USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), a Nimitz-class nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, is shown at Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, Calif., on Aug. 11, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Warren went on to say that the U.S. should not "spend another cent" on the war in Iran, noting the total estimated cost of the war provided by the Pentagon is over $47 billion.

Cao urged lawmakers to approve further funding for the Navy throughout Tuesday's hearing. He argued that the U.S. is in a "1939 moment," and must "be able to build like we did back in World War II."

THIRD US AIRCRAFT CARRIER ARRIVES IN MIDDLE EAST AS IRAN RULES OUT UN NUCLEAR INSPECTIONS

He said the U.S. Navy currently has roughly 280 active vessels, but he said the country needs to surge up to 355.

U.S. Central Command released this photo on Feb. 24, saying, "Sailors and Marines aboard USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) regularly perform maintenance to keep aircraft mission-ready." (CENTCOM)

Several lawmakers shared concerns about reports of poor morale and mental health among sailors due to long deployments for the Iran war. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., highlighted eight suicide attempts aboard vessels in the USS Abraham Lincoln's carrier strike group, blasting Cao's characterization that there had been eight "mitigated" suicides.

Cao argued that the long deployments seen in the Iran war are due to a lack of available vessels, once again urging lawmakers to approve funding to bolster U.S. fleets.

Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Finland’s Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
excerpt: ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio...
body_text:
ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business.

The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China.

“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday.

The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.

The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.”

Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it.

Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.

Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production.

Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs.

An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval.

In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers.

Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.

Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.

Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.

“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.

With material from Reuters by Giulia Segreti and Essi Lehto.

title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
excerpt:
Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law

The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it us...
body_text:
Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law

The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.

Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.

FracTracker contends this exemption contradicts the widely held definition of production, including that implied in Colorado’s regulatory literature.

Legislators who authored the law, public health groups, and industry all use definitions of “production” that includes drilling, FracTracker states, and it notes the law requires “disclosure of all chemicals used underground or ‘downhole’ in oil and gas wells”.

Meanwhile, at least five chemicals that were reported for use in fracking are prohibited by Colorado law, FracTracker alleges. It also found fossil-fuel companies reported using at least three highly toxic chemicals that raise serious safety questions.

About 43,000 people live within a mile of the state’s wells, and many within a few hundred feet. Regulators are flying blind on what the sum impact of the chemicals may be, the authors allege.

“This is a public health crisis and it should be treated as such,” Shannon Smith, FracTracker’s executive director, told the Guardian. FracTacker is a non-profit that investigates and monitors public health threats created by the fossil-fuel industry, and advocates for protections. It began in Pennsylvania in 2010, but now organizes nationally.

Fracking operators and their suppliers are supposed to disclose all downhole chemical ingredients to the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) regulatory agency within 150 days. The agency then must post the chemicals on its website.

ECMC literature implies the agency considers drilling as part of oil and gas production. In a statement, an ECMC spokesperson said the agency was “aware of differing views regarding the scope and implementation of the chemical disclosure requirements”.

“We are applying the law and Commission rules under the current statutory and regulatory framework while continuing to work with stakeholders to clarify these issues and support consistent, appropriate implementation,” the spokesperson said.

Halliburton, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the state’s top fossil-fuel producers.

In a statement, a Chevron spokesperson said the company “is committed to safe and responsible operations in Colorado”.

“We take chemical-disclosure requirements seriously and remain focused on meeting our obligations and maintaining transparent, responsible operating practices,” the spokesperson added.

In order to drill wells and extract minerals, fossil-fuel operators pump huge volumes of pressurized liquid into the earth to fracture – or “frack” – bedrock, stimulating the release of trapped oil and gas. These fluids are mostly water and sand by volume, but they also contain industrial chemicals, including biocides, surfactants and lubricants.

Hundreds of studies have pointed to health risks for those in fracking regions. Toxic chemicals such as formaldehyde, Pfas and benzene have been widely detected or reported in fracking fluids. These and other chemicals used – or thought to be used – in production are linked to issues such as cancer, hormone disruption and neurological damage.

Gas companies reported as many as 11 spills a week in 2018, and people are exposed to the chemicals through multiple pathways, including groundwater, above ground spills, wastewater seepage into drinking water supplies, and air emissions.

The ECMC has told FracTracker that it does not consider drilling to be part of the fracking and production said the report’s author, Dusty Horwitt, FracTracker’s senior research and policy counsel.

“That was news to us, and it is not consistent with The American Petroleum Institute definition of what oil and gas production is,” Horwitt added. API literature shows oil and gas production includes “drilling, extraction, and recovery of oil from underground”.

Meg Froelich, the Colorado state representative who co-wrote the 2022 legislation, said she intended for drilling chemicals to be disclosed. The legislation is called “Concerning enhanced oversight of the chemicals used in oil and gas production.” Production includes drilling, Froelich said.

She accused the ECMC of “word-parsing” and added that she was “mad about their stalling”.

“The law covers everything that goes downhole because everything that goes downhole has the potential to affect neighbors,” Froelich told the Guardian.

The ECMC until recent years has largely worked to promote the fossil-fuel industry, and only since Democrats took over the state government has it shifted to also protect public health, but the shift has come in “fits and starts”, Froelich said.

State records show that wells covered by law operated without drilling chemical disclosure for at least a collective 843,369 days from the rules’ implementation to May 16, when the analysis was conducted.

The law also requires fossil-fuel companies to provide schools, first responders and other community institutions with lists of chemicals it uses, but it has failed to do that, advocates say.

The report comes after a previous analysis reported on by the Guardian found Colorado fossil-fuel companies pumped at least 30m lb of secret chemicals into the ground over an 18-month period without making legally required disclosures. Out of over 1,100 fracked sites across the state, companies did not disclose 675, or about 60%.

Since then, the compliance rate is closer to 100% – except for the drilling chemicals, advocates say.

The report raises questions about which chemicals are being used for drilling. A recent law banned any use of Pfas at oil and gas sites, and industry literature and peer-reviewed research suggests that Pfas are a common drilling chemical. Horwitt told the Guardian he fears the chemicals may be used in Colorado.

“Publications, including those issued by major oil and gas-producing nations Canada and Norway, report that PFAS is used for multiple purposes in oil and gas production including drilling and enhanced oil recovery,” FracTracker states. The lack of drilling chemical disclosure in Colorado “creates uncertainty about whether companies are complying with the PFAS ban”, the report added.

Meanwhile, records from Ohio show the frequent use of xylene, the report states. The chemical can cause headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of muscle coordination, and, in high doses, death.

FracTracker also points to five chemicals that were disclosed as being used for fracking on some well pads despite state rules prohibiting their use in fracking: 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol, 1,4-dioxane, N,N-dimethylformamide and BMPA. Some of these compounds are linked to cancer, liver disease, and harm to developing children.

In its statement, the ECMC said it had “issued notices of alleged violation when prohibited substances are identified, including cases involving 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol and 1,4-dioxane”.

Among potentially harmful chemicals that are permitted are acrylamide, ethylene oxide and methanol. FracTracker noted that those were among the chemicals disclosed as being used in a well in Galeton that sprayed a geyser of gas and at least 3.7m gallons of fluid for over four days in April 2025.

Living near wells has well-established links to leukemia, birth abnormalities and other serious health problems. Residents in July reported to the Guardian that they are plagued by loud noise, acrid air emissions, headaches, nosebleeds and respiratory issues.

title: More than 100,000 take part in France pay protests
excerpt:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the high cost of living, with public sector workers demanding pay increases.

The Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that...
body_text:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the high cost of living, with public sector workers demanding pay increases.

The Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that a total of 146,000 people took part in the protests, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.

Several trade unions had called for a day of strike action. Participants included public sector workers, as well as school pupils and university students.

France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were pushed to mobilise after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands. Union representatives left the meeting organised by Lecornu saying the proposed measures failed to address the urgency of the pay situation.

Tuesday’s rally is the third call for a united day of action and strikes in the public sector since September.

Unions have been pushing for across-the-board pay rises since last week’s boost to the minimum wage for private-sector workers.

Protesters say “they simply can’t make ends meet, and they want the government to help them put more money into funding in terms of salaries, in terms of raising the minimum wage”, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reported from Paris.

“The government’s already offered about $30 extra a month on the minimum wage, but those here say that is simply not enough. With inflation, with the way the prices are going up, they say they actually need more.”

The unions put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.

“The government doesn’t have much margin or wiggle room financially, because of France’s ballooning debt, and the government’s in the middle of trying to push through a budget with cost-cutting measures in it,” Butler said.

Public-sector workers aim to pressure the government to unfreeze the pay scale point used to calculate their basic salary. However, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year in its draft budget.

“The people in the street know there is only so far you can go; the government knows they do not have a lot of economic wiggle room. Yet nobody really is coming up with another solution,” Butler said.

Despite the government’s efforts to ease tensions, demonstrations have roiled the country for over a month.

Student-led protests demanding better conditions in education erupted in mid-September, but the movement has since expanded in scope to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing

Protests for higher wages, lower costs of living and better public services have also spread across Europe.

title: Children linked to religious sect raided by UK police now subject of care proceedings
excerpt:
Scale of cases in family court relating to Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light ‘rarely seen before’, one lawyer said

Scores of children linked to a religious sect raided by police over allegations of ...
body_text:
Scale of cases in family court relating to Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light ‘rarely seen before’, one lawyer said

Scores of children linked to a religious sect raided by police over allegations of serious sexual offences and modern slavery are now the subject of care proceedings, court documents have revealed.

Family courts were dealing with more than 40 cases in relation to “a very significant number of children” who were living at the compound run by the Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light (AROPL) when it was raided by police in April.

The findings can be reported after the courts overturned requests from AROPL members to stop the judgment being published.

The scale of the cases going through the family courts had “rarely been seen before”, a family lawyer said. They accounted for almost one in 20 care cases at the family court in Manchester.

More than 100 people were living at Webb House, a former orphanage in Crewe, north-west England, used as AROPL’s headquarters. The sect blends tenets of Islam with conspiracy theories about the Illuminati and aliens controlling US presidents.

Police have since arrested 14 people on suspicion of offences including human trafficking, sexual assault, rape, forced marriage and modern day slavery. One suspect has been released with no further action.

Cheshire constabulary has stressed that it is investigating individual people and not the sect as a whole. But the force said the raid raised concerns in relation to the welfare of children who were members of the group.

A judgment from Mr Justice Hayden in the Manchester family court published on Tuesday in the case of two of the children laid out a series of concerns from police and social services.

Representatives from the local authority told the court that conditions in the dormitories where children reportedly lived were “observed to be neglectful with dirty bedding”. CCTV cameras were found inside the children’s dormitories.

Concerns were raised about the educational provision for the children in the group. The court heard that most of them were home schooled via computer screens.

Knives were recovered during the police raid along with a sharps bin, suggesting injections may have been administered outside of a registered medical setting.

The ruling, which was handed down in June but published only on Tuesday, dismissed one parent’s attempt to appeal against the interim order granted by a judge. Interim orders are issued during care proceedings. They grant the local authority, in this case Cheshire East council, shared parental responsibility for the children.

The mother argued that she was choosing to remain with the group and felt that the court order meant she was “being dictated how I am to live my life and who is able to live with me”.

Hayden found there was no legitimate reason to dismiss the orders while the family court cases were ongoing, a process that may take months.

The majority of children from AROPL who are now under interim care orders have remained with their families while the court examines their cases. None of them are still living at the group’s headquarters.

Alex O’Dwyer Curran, a family lawyer from Payne Hicks Beach who is not involved in the proceedings, said there was “little doubt about the sheer scale of this litigation”, adding that “it is difficult to identify a comparable case in the history of the modern family court”.

Lawyers for the families involved sought to prevent publication of details relating to the care orders of the children. They argued publication of the judgment would put “significant new information into the public domain” and could “reheat the hostility to the community, and risk exposing children and parents to physical and emotional harm and potential public disorder”.

Media organisations, including the Guardian and Press Association, resisted the attempt to stop the judgment being published.

In his rejection of the application, Hayden wrote: “The court cannot simply close its doors in response to unspecified concerns about potential civil disorder.”

The Guardian has previously reported that former residents of the site had expressed concerns about the wellbeing and education of the children there.

Cheshire East council’s social services have twice made inquiries relating to the group or the children in the past. There is no evidence to suggest that action was deemed necessary on those occasions.

Two relatives of a teenager living at the Crewe premises have previously told the Guardian that the teenager told them he was unhappy living with the group and wanted to leave. His family members said they were concerned that he was not in formal education but was being home schooled at the site.

AROPL’s lawyer said at the time that the organisation was not involved in home schooling, which was led by parents. The group had considered setting up a formal school, the lawyer said, but had shelved the idea and dismantled classrooms inside Webb House.

AROPL followers are warned about the corrupting influence of mainstream education on children and are encouraged to “take advantage of laws” in countries that enable home schooling.

title: NSA attributes US network outage to routine ‘maintenance’ activities
excerpt:
The United States National Security Agency (NSA) has said an outage affecting its internal communications network was due to “routine maintenance”, following a report by CNN.

The report, published on...
body_text:
The United States National Security Agency (NSA) has said an outage affecting its internal communications network was due to “routine maintenance”, following a report by CNN.

The report, published on Tuesday and citing six unnamed sources, said there was no evidence that the outage was the result of a cyberattack. The incident follows a series of outages that have gone without explanation in recent days.

The network, known as NSA Net, allows employees of the US surveillance agency to share highly classified information internally, CNN said.

A spokesperson for the NSA downplayed the outage in a statement to Al Jazeera

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the statement said. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational, and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

The reported network disruption at the NSA follows several other major outages that have affected communication and transportation services in the US.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted all takeoffs in the country on Friday, claiming that a system upgrade caused a flight communication overload. The nearly four-hour ground stop, it explained, was called out of an “abundance of caution”.

The tech giant Microsoft also announced that services such as Outlook and Teams were down last week.

More recently, on Monday, outages hit major banks, and United Airlines briefly suffered a system disruption that delayed some departing flights.

US President Donald Trump has played down the seriousness of those outages.

“Things like that happen,” Trump told reporters on Tuesday. “It’s fine.”

title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down
excerpt:
NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails

The National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporar...
body_text:
NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails

The National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down.

In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events.

The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored.

The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily.

The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said.

Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff.

A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong.

The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights, a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible.

Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.”

He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions.

title: College basketball picks for Tuesday: Duke vs. Illinois, Michigan State vs. Tennessee and more best bets
excerpt: "Great college basketball game a couple nights ago. In your building, Indiana versus my alma mater, Syracuse. Empty. Empty. An embarrassment to the once legendary Indiana basketball program. And may c...
body_text:
"Great college basketball game a couple nights ago. In your building, Indiana versus my alma mater, Syracuse. Empty. Empty. An embarrassment to the once legendary Indiana basketball program. And may coach Knight rest in peace and may Isiah Thomas rest in peace. I know he's alive. How do you not sell out Indiana vs. Syracuse? It looks like a WNBA game."

Tuesday is the first college basketball card of the season that feels like it matters. Two top-10 teams meet in Durham, Michigan State brings its Duke-beating defense into Knoxville to battle Tennessee, and the undercard is full of spots where the betting market has guessed wrong.

I’ve got four plays, starting at 4:30 p.m. and running later into the night. Some of them back the favorite, and some take the points. All of them come down to the same idea: trust what the numbers say, not the names on the front of the jerseys.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Fifteen and a half points is a lot to give a team that shoots like Notre Dame.

The Irish rank first in the country in three-point percentage at 47.8%, and they’re shooting 50.4% from the field overall. Teams that shoot that well from deep don’t fall behind by 16 very often. Even when they’re losing, a couple of late threes keeps the backdoor wide open.

Notre Dame has also been one of the most reliable bets in the sport after a cover, going 6-0-1 against the spread in its last seven games following an ATS win. The Irish are coming in with five days of rest, compared with three for Florida.

The concern is the glass, where Florida ranks 36th in rebounding and Notre Dame ranks 180th. If the Gators control the boards, this could get away from the Irish. But a team that shoots this well doesn’t need many possessions to cover a 15.5-point spread.

Florida head coach Todd Golden reacts during the first half in the second round of the NCAA college basketball tournament against Connecticut, Sunday, March 23, 2025, in Raleigh, N.C. (AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough)

Everyone loves Illinois this week, and I understand why. The Illini have the most efficient offense in the country. They’ve made 75% of their two-point attempts and topped 108 points three times. Andrej Stojakovic is averaging 22.3 points per game on 61.8% shooting.

But Illinois is walking into Cameron Indoor, and Duke is still upset about Michigan State.

Duke ranks second nationally in overall efficiency and third on both offense and defense. Opponents are averaging 57 points per game against the Blue Devils, and three of their four opponents have scored 52 or fewer. Duke is 3-0 at home and 3-1 against the spread.

Illinois’ defense is the weak spot. The Illini allow 71.3 points per game and just gave up 86 to Sam Houston. They’re 0-1 on the road, having lost 84-78 at Texas Tech, and they’ll be without forward David Mirkovic, who’s out after an appendectomy.

The public sees the best offense in America getting 7.5 points. I see an elite defense at home, with a week to think about its only loss.

Duke Blue Devils head coach Jon Scheyer reacts in the first half at Dean E. Smith Center on Feb. 7, 2026. (Bob Donnan/Imagn Images)

This is the matchup I’m playing twice, because both bets rely on the same weakness.

Tennessee is 3-0, but those wins came against the 336th-ranked schedule in the country. The Vols are shooting under 31% from three. Their 302nd ranking in offensive block percentage means opponents are swatting their shots at the rim, too. Now they face a Michigan State defense that ranks fifth in adjusted efficiency and ninth in block percentage.

Michigan State is also built to win the possession battle. The Spartans rank fifth in offensive rebounding percentage, and Tennessee ranks 258th in defensive rebounding. That’s a lot of second chances for Michigan State. Jeremy Fears Jr. is the best player on the floor, and the Spartans already proved they can win a big road-style game by beating Duke.

The total comes down to style, not star power. Tennessee’s defense is legitimate, ranking 29th in adjusted efficiency and allowing 61.3 points per game. Michigan State gives up 66.3. Two physical, deliberate teams with one offense that can’t hit a three is a recipe for a game in the 130s.

title: Ukraine drone attack kills two in Crimea as Kyiv targets bridge to Russia
excerpt: A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive ...
body_text:
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive day, according to the Moscow-installed governor.

In a Telegram post, Sergei Aksyonov said traffic has been suspended after Tuesday’s attack on the Kerch Bridge.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the “unprecedented” attack, publishing footage on social media on Tuesday that showed the main arch of the bridge for cars and part of its roadway collapsed.

He said the targeting came in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure.

The bridge in the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, stretches for 19km (11.8 miles) and is also used by trains.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said Russia came under one of the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Monday night.

“According to official data from the Ministry of Defence, Russian air defence systems destroyed more than 1,400 drones over 23 regions, including border regions and regions in central Russia. Meanwhile, the mayor of Moscow said that more than 800 drones flew towards the capital,” Shapovalova reported.

Also on Tuesday, Moscow attacked two bridges in Kyiv, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a Telegram post that ⁠the Northern and ⁠Southern bridges had been hit and the subway ⁠system ⁠had also been damaged. He added that water and power supplies had been ‌partially cut.

The Russian Defence Ministry said it also targeted Ukraine’s military infrastructure in attacks on Monday night, including facilities used to produce cruise missiles and long‑ and medium‑range drones. The ministry said transport and energy facilities were also targeted as well as port infrastructure and ships used by the Ukrainian military.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the first of a “series of very loud explosions” rang out in Kyiv just before midnight.

“Another round of explosions was heard just after 5am [03:00 GMT] this morning,” she said.

“Some bridges were damaged. We understand that they are still standing, but there is no traffic on either of them. These are bridges that are used every day by civilians to commute around the city. These attacks also cut heating to hundreds of apartment buildings on Kyiv’s Left Bank.”

The exchange of attacks comes just days before a meeting of Presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia, Xi Jinping of China and Donald Trump of the United States in China’s Shenzhen region.

The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Thursday’s talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.

Trump has made securing an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine a key part of his presidency. Despite another round of talks held in the United Arab Emirates last week, US mediators have failed to make a breakthrough.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Kyiv would carry out attacks on Russia in the days before the meeting.

title: Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
excerpt:
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspe...
body_text:
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.

South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.

These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.

The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".

The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.

Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.

South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.

It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.

The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.

Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.

Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.

For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.

In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.
