title: Bob Dylan's hooded Vatican visit with Pope Leo shows he's still knockin' on heaven's door
excerpt:
Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

I was not surprised to see legendary singer and songwriter Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman) visiting Po...
body_text:
Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

I was not surprised to see legendary singer and songwriter Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman) visiting Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican a few weeks ago, dressed in what looked to be nomadic garb. He reportedly insisted on keeping his hood up, and the pope agreed. Perhaps Dylan was channeling his apocalyptic song "All Along the Watchtower," which describes the fall of Babylon prophesied in the eighth century (Isaiah 21) before taking place in 539 B.C. Or perhaps he was taking on the role of a hooded healer to the pope, who had just recovered from lung cancer surgery.

It is no secret that Pope Leo, who hails from Chicago, is a longtime fan of Dylan’s, another Midwesterner who was born in Duluth, Minnesota. In July 2026, the pope wrote the preface for a Vatican book called "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." In it, he quoted from Dylan’s unreleased 1963 Cold War protest song, "Go Away You Bomb": "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled."

At the meeting with Dylan, the pope pointed to his Augustinian background (he is the first Augustinian friar to be elected pope) and introduced himself as a "son of St. Augustine." This was no doubt a direct reference to Dylan’s 1967 song, "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine."

POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS

According to Dylan’s longtime Chabad rabbi, Manis Friedman, Dylan is a spiritual seeker. "The answer is blowin’ in the wind," Friedman told me for my new book, "The Angels Among Us," "but Dylan hasn’t found it yet. He’s knockin’ on heaven’s door, but can’t get in."

Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

Indeed, Dylan’s deep spiritual journeys and investigations reflect this "seeking" as he ranges from Orthodox Judaism to evangelical Christianity (he famously saw Jesus in a hotel room in 1978 and studied the New Testament intensely with his then-girlfriend, Mary Alice Artes, from 1978 to 1980).

DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED

During this born-again Christian period, Dylan produced his celebrated album "Slow Train Coming," including the hit song "Gotta Serve Somebody," followed by "Every Grain of Sand" on his album "Shot of Love."

An image of  Fox News contributor Dr. Marc Siegel's new book 'The Angels Among Us' (Fox Books)

But while Dylan was studying the New Testament, he was introduced to Rabbi Friedman as well as the famed Rebbe (Rabbi Menachem Schneerson), and Dylan then refocused his studies to include the Old Testament. As I write in my new book, he asked Rabbi Friedman, "What does infidel mean? He liked the word, kept asking about it. Infidel? What did I think of it?"

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

Dylan was once again questioning and reforming his spiritual identity, this time more toward Orthodox Judaism. The album "Infidels" followed in 1983, including the song "Jokerman," about a worker of blasphemous magic, more of an Antichrist than a godlike figure.

One of Dylan’s best friends from childhood was Larry Kegan, who was paralyzed in a cliff-diving accident at age 16 but managed to survive as he said a prayer directly to God. He spent the rest of his life as a psychotherapist giving back to God and humanity, and he became Bob Dylan’s angel, often appearing with him at concerts in a wheelchair. As I describe in "The Angels Among Us," when Dylan, Larry and a third friend visited the Rebbe, with thousands in the room, everyone ignored the famous Dylan as the Rebbe had eyes only for Larry. The Rebbe raised a glass and wished Larry Kegan a long life. Dylan was humbled, saying he needed to work on his soul so he could become more worthy of recognition.

POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY

This meeting with the pope wasn’t Dylan’s first. In 1997, he nearly died of a severe infection known as pericardial histoplasmosis, especially difficult for a smoker to recover from. Coincidentally, Dylan recorded his near-death song, "Not Dark Yet," months before he got sick. A few months after he recovered, Dylan met with Pope John Paul II in Bologna, Italy, a meeting that Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (the future Pope Benedict XVI) tried to block because, as he wrote later in his memoirs, he considered rock stars like Dylan to be the wrong kind of "prophet" for Christian youth. But Pope John Paul II overruled him, and Dylan performed several songs, including "Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door."

After the performance, the pope addressed the crowd and took on the very question that Dylan raised in "Blowin’ in the Wind" that Rabbi Friedman mentioned.

The pope had a definitive answer: "A representative of yours has spoken for you, saying that the answer is 'blowin' in the wind.' It is true! But not in the wind that blows things away in a whirlwind of nothingness. The wind that is the breath and voice of the Spirit, a voice that calls and says: 'Come!' You asked me: how many roads must a man walk down before you can call him a man? I answer you: one! There is only one road for man, and it is the road of Jesus Christ, who said, 'I am the way.'"

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR MARC SIEGEL

Marc Siegel, M.D. is a professor of medicine and medical director of Doctor Radio at NYU Langone Medical Center. He is Fox News Channel's senior medical analyst. His forthcoming book is "The Angels Among Us: How God's Messengers Play a Role in Healing." (Fox Books, November 17, 2026). His previous book "The Miracles Among Us: How God's Grace Plays a Role in Healing" (Fox Books, November 18, 2025)  debuted at #1 on both the New York Times and Publisher’s Weekly bestseller lists. He is also the author of "COVID: The Politics of Fear and the Power of Science." Follow him on X @drmarcsiegel.

title: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
excerpt:
Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli c...
body_text:
Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.

The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.

Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.

Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.

The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.

On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.

The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.

The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”

But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.

According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining items that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

title: Milburn calls for welfare state ‘revolution’ as landmark youth unemployment report to be published – UK politics live
excerpt:
Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Alan Milbur...
body_text:
Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Alan Milburn told Sky News this morning that Labour MPs have so far welcomed his proposals.

When Keir Starmer’s government proposed cutting disability benefits last year, there was a huge backbench rebellion and it was forced to back down.

As Pippa Crerar explains here, Milburn has learned lessons from this debacle. He has spent months making a moral and welfare argument for his plans (unlike Starmer and Rachel Reeves, who tried to justify their cuts principally on cost-cutting grounds), and all the signs so far suggest this has paid off.

Milburn said he received an “incredibly positive” response at the meeting with Labour MPs because they recognised there was a “moral imperative” to act, as well as the economic benefits.

Labour MPs “have to vote for it”, he said.

double quotation markLabour is what it says on the tin. It’s the party of work. It’s not the party of welfare and of benefits.

Defending his plan to cut some benefits to fund much better employment support instead, he said:

double quotation markThere will be some young people who are worse off at least initially as a consequence of benefit changes. But in the end, the best thing for people is to get them into work.

There’s so many young people, for example, who come into the welfare system who frankly shouldn’t be there. It’s not inevitable that if somebody has got anxiety or depression or moderate ADHD, that somehow we should be saying to them, ‘What can’t you do?’

Why aren’t we asking them, ‘What could you do? What could we help you do? What is the opportunity that we can provide for you?’

And so that’s what we should do. And that’s why we need this revolution in the welfare state.

More than 300,000 children across Britain are no longer defined as living in poverty, following the government’s decision to scrap the two-child limit for one of the main types of welfare, figures show. The Press Association says:

double quotation markUnder previous rules, families could only receive the child element of universal credit for their first two children.

Universal credit (UC) is the main form of means-tested social security in the UK and is intended to help with living costs for people in work who are on low incomes, as well as those who are unemployed or cannot work.

The decision to scrap the two-child limit for UC was announced by former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the budget in November 2025 and came into effect in April 2026.

Analysis published today by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) estimates that 301,720 children in Britain are no longer living in households below the poverty line, due to the removal of the UC cap.

Households where income is less than 60% of the median national average, after housing costs, are considered to be living in poverty.

The figures also show 118,630 adults are no longer defined as living in households in poverty, because of the lifting of the two-child rule.

Overall, 1.57 million children are in families that have seen a rise in UC payments since April, including those no longer below the poverty line.

Commenting on the figures, Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said:

double quotation markThis is about changing the story of children’s lives.

Children who grow up in poverty are more likely to have mental health difficulties, to be Neet and to earn less as adults.

We want to give every child a genuine shot at life – to do well at school, stay healthy, succeed at work – ultimately contributing to their community as adults.

Removing the two-child limit is the most cost-effective way to drive down child poverty rates and is an investment worth making – for those children, for their families, and for the whole country.

This is what the opposition parties have been saying about the Alan Milburn proposals. The full report has not formally been published yet, but it has been circulating in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday and so the parties all know what it says.

The Conservatives says Milburn should be cutting welfare more aggressively. This is from Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary.

double quotation markConservatives agree with Alan Milburn on the problem, and we want his review to succeed. Where Milburn gets it right, we’ll back him. Especially where he adopts our proposals like shifting from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and cutting national insurance for young people.

Alan Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now - because nothing will happen for at least three years.

The Liberal Democrats say they would prefer a proper plan for growth, including joining the single market. Ed Davey, the party leader, says:

double quotation markSuccessive governments have allowed a generation to fall through the cracks. Nearly a million young people are now out of work or training, which is more than there are job vacancies in the entire country. ‘Work not welfare’ means nothing when the work simply isn’t there.

If ministers want to halve the number of Neets by 2036, they need a plan for growth. That means scrapping Labour’s jobs tax, joining the EU single market and cutting the cost of doing business, so firms can afford to hire young people again. No target or guarantee can conjure up jobs that don’t exist.

Reform UK says Milburn is admitting Labour’s policies have failed. Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson, says:

double quotation markAlan Milburn’s call to cut the cost of hiring for employers is a glaring admission Labour’s jobs tax has failed. It destroyed opportunities for workers, and particularly youngsters. Huge amounts of damage could have been avoided if Labour listened to the warnings.

Waiting 10 years to fix the youth jobs crisis is a huge missed opportunity. We would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap.

Reform UK would act now to axe Labour’s jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt.

The Green party says its Youth Jobs guarantee is a much better offer for young people. Mothin Ali, its co-deputy leader, says:

double quotation markWhat we’ve seen so far from the Blair-era minister and adviser to private equity firms is extremely concerning. There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work.

Andy Burnham promised an end to 40 years of neoliberalism, but this is more of the same tired proposals. The Green party’s true alternative is proper work and training for proper pay, so young people can reach their full potential without the threat of poverty and homelessness.

The Greens have also posted this on social media.

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution, Patrick Wintour reports.

Alan Milburn told Sky News that his report recommends paying small businesses £5,000 if they take on a young person who is Neet (not in education, employment or training). He said:

double quotation markWhat we need to do is make it more worthwhile for employers to take on more young people. So we say in this report, if you’re a small business, for example, the government should give you a £5,000 payment for taking on a young person who is Neet to help you absorb the costs of their hiring.

And so that’s what we should do. And that’s why we need this revolution in the welfare state.

The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release the Alan Milburn report on the youth jobs crisis, Phillip Inman reports.

Good morning. Few government reports have been as long-awaited and well-trailed as the Alan Milburn report into youth unemployment, or Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), that is finally being published this morning. The title, From a Welfare State to a Working State, gives a clue as to the extent of Milburn’s ambition and, if it gets implemented in full, it will be remembered as one of the landmark social reforms of the 21st century (so far).

And even if Milburn only achieves 50% of what he wants (which, sadly, is probably quite a good success rate for the authors of independent government reports), he will change Britain significantly, as Polly Toynbee argues in a must-read column about the report today. She says:

double quotation markThere will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.”

Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area.

Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool, Merseyside Youth Association. Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free …

It’s for Labour and Milburn, who will remain in post to oversee all of this, to prove, with falling Neet numbers, the value of good social investment. If even half these plans work, that will be a great social advance – a generational shift from appeasing the old to finally directing hope and resources towards the young. And it will be about time.

The full report is being published this morning. But it won’t contain any surprises – Milburn has been talking about his proposals for weeks now, and all the main ideas are already in the public domain. Here is our overnight story by Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu.

So far, none of the reaction from the charity sector has been particularly hostile. The opposition parties have generally welcomed the bits of the plan that overlap with their own policies, while criticising the rest. But, for the government, the reaction that matters the most will come in the Commons, when Labour MPs get the chance to say what they think.

Milburn has been giving interviews this morning. And he has claimed that, under his plan, the government could start to save money from the welfare budget before the end of this parliament. This is an important pledge because John Healey, the chancellor, was criticised recently by the Tories for failing to propose cutting benefits before the next election.

double quotation markWe should be doing that. We can get the benefits bill down. And by the way, we can do that quickly. We can start in this parliament to get savings from welfare. But what we’ve got to do is start creating opportunities and support for young people.

But those savings would not at first offset the extra government spending his plan would require. Milburn says his proposals would require “an immediate upfront payment” of £500m in the next financial year.

On the Today programme, Milburn argued that, over time, his plan would save money. He explained:

double quotation markWe can either get the benefits bill down through crude cuts. And when that happens, all that then happens is more young people are in destitution and poverty and frankly will show up somewhere else on the ledger in more housing costs or health costs or crime costs.

Or we can do it through more jobs. And my view is that it’s got to be more jobs.

And over time then, what happens by the time the 10-year programme gets to a conclusion, we will have saved about £13.8bn in welfare.

Milburn was referring to the amount saved from the welfare budget. His plans would require extra spending in other areas, and his plan would involve around £5.8bn a year of funding by 2036-37, offset by £3.6bn of welfare savings and £2.4bn of extra tax revenue from people in work.

When it was put to him that in the short term, his plan “costs, doesn’t save”, Milburn replied: “Correct.” And when it was put to him that the “crossover point” when overall savings would overtake overall costs would only happen after 10 years, Milburn replied: “That’s when it happens.”

9.30am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where Alan Milburn will speak about his youth unemployment report.

9.30am: The Department for Work and Pensions publishes quarterly universal credit figures.

Morning: Kemi Badenoch and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, are on a visit in London.

10.30am: Marsha de Cordova MP and Sandro Gozi MEP, co-chairs of the UK-EU Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, hold a press conference after its meeting in London.

11.30am: Milburn holds a press conference to mark the publication of his report.

11.30am: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 12.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, is due to give a statement to MPs about the Milburn report.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

title: Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
excerpt:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operatio...
body_text:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to china.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

The Northern Bridge (pictured in October) is closed after being targeted again by Russia

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war

Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing

Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks

title: Fomula One champion Fernando Alonso to race at Dakar Rally 2027
excerpt:
Double Formula One champion Fernando Alonso says he will compete at the upcoming Dakar Rally, making his return to the race after seven years.

The 45-year-old Spaniard, a 32-time Grand Prix winner an...
body_text:
Double Formula One champion Fernando Alonso says he will compete at the upcoming Dakar Rally, making his return to the race after seven years.

The 45-year-old Spaniard, a 32-time Grand Prix winner and two-time Le Mans 24 Hours winner, announced his intention to race in the annual on Tuesday and said he will work with an Aston ⁠Martin Dreadnought entry run by engineering partner Prodrive.

He competed at the Dakar Rally in 2020 with Toyota and finished 13th.

“In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula One and the Dakar Rally in the same year,” he explained in a statement.

“In 2020, Dakar was one of the most challenging and enjoyable experiences of my career. I have enormous ⁠respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it.”

The 49th edition of the Dakar Rally will be held in Morocco from January 9 to 23, with a prologue and first stage in Portugal, after being moved from Saudi Arabia due to security concerns.

The 24-round Formula One season is due to start in Bahrain ‌in March after testing in late February.

Alonso, who will again have compatriot and five-time motorcycle Dakar winner Marc Coma as co-driver, is racing in the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend. He said he had turned his thoughts to Dakar after deciding to continue in Formula One with Aston Martin.

“Formula One remains my priority. ⁠But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve.”

France’s ⁠nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb and Brazil’s reigning world rally-raid champion Lucas Moraes will be his teammates in a three-car entry.

The Dakar will be ‌Aston Martin Racing’s debut in the world rally-raid championship.

title: Former WH Smith chain TG Jones put up for sale after closing 130 stores
excerpt:
Modella Capital plans auction of high street retailer, which employs about 3,500 people, next year

The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing a deal to b...
body_text:
Modella Capital plans auction of high street retailer, which employs about 3,500 people, next year

The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing a deal to buy the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith.

Modella Capital, which also owns businesses including Hobbycraft, completed a deal to buy the 233-year-old business for £76m in June last year.

The company, which pushed through a swingeing restructure to close more than 100 stores after receiving high court approval in July, has moved to appoint advisers after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest for the business.

Modella, which has closed about 150 of the 480 WH Smith stores since taking control, has appointed the corporate finance arm of Teneo, according to Sky News which first reported the news.

“High-street retailer TG Jones has received unsolicited offers for the business,” said Modella and TG Jones in a joint statement. “Management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo Corporate Finance to review these offers and undertake a market-testing exercise.”

An auction of the business, which employs about 3,500 staff, is planned for next year to avoid disruption through the key Christmas trading period.

“As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up,” said the TG Jones chief executive, Alex Wilson. “We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month.”

WH Smith retained its almost 1,300 stores in train stations and airports, as well as its website and the right to its name, promoting the rebrand of the high street stores to TG Jones.

The potential sale comes as the future of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, remains uncertain.

Last week the chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors as it assesses three potential bids.

Last month its US owners filed a notice of intention to call in administrators, but has come under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers.

title: Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
excerpt:
Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ but Kremlin claims bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia ...
body_text:
Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ but Kremlin claims bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.

“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective,” he wrote. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

Earlier, Russian forces struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.

The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted on Telegram.

He added: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, after which one of the country’s deputy prime ministers, Marat Khusnullin, briefed Putin on the damage to the bridge, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.

Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.

But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.

“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

The Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.

He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”

Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on Fire”, a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.

Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.

The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.

Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.

Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.

Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway.

Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.

Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.

A Russian missile attack injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.

The ministry ​said the strikes also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.

Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner ​said progress had been ‌made towards an ​agreement, though important ​challenges remain to end the war, which Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

title: Schumer boasts early advantage in Senate power struggle as Dem rival warns against 'coronation'
excerpt:
Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to analyze the growing progressive push for a sweeping legislative agenda on Capitol Hill.

With a historic race to be the ...
body_text:
Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to analyze the growing progressive push for a sweeping legislative agenda on Capitol Hill.

With a historic race to be the top Senate Democrat locked in, both candidates eyeing the job of leading Democrats into their majority believe they have a path to victory.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has raised a challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to steer Democrats through the final two years of President Donald Trump’s time in office.

It’s the first time in three decades that the race has been contested, and both believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader. But neither has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number.

DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Both Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., are confident they have the votes to lead Democrats, but Schumer, so far, has the lead in public endorsements. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images; Alex Brandon-Pool/Getty Images)

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, making him the clear front-runner.

The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," but asserted, "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."

Schumer’s allies, like Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., argue that he has led Senate Democrats to a 55-seat majority, which could expand by another seat if Alaska flips.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Van Hollen, who acknowledged that he is the "underdog," has five public backers who can vote in the forthcoming leadership elections — Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who is retiring, is backing Van Hollen but doesn’t have a vote.

His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races.

Van Hollen, however, argued that he has as many as 15 in his corner. He also alleged in an interview with Politico that Democrats were trying to move up the Dec. 1 secret-ballot leadership election to kneecap his chances.

"Let’s not rush into a coronation," Van Hollen said.

Fox News Digital reached out for comment from Van Hollen and Schumer’s offices about Van Hollen's claim.

SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver on Nov. 13, 2026, as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Schumer is playing the quiet game, Van Hollen has launched a public push for the job, making several appearances across the gamut of cable news and launching his own website declaring that voters’ backing of Democrats across the country was a rejection of the "status quo," and that "to deliver, we need new leadership."

There’s also a request for donations on the site, raising questions about Van Hollen’s future ambitions. He initially was "kicking the tires" on a 2028 bid for the White House, but since then, he has dropped the idea.

Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump.

"I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver.

But it raises the question whether a leadership bid is a launch pad for higher office.

"At a minimum, it’s good for his base fundraising," a Democratic source told Fox News Digital.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
excerpt:
The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties.

In a statement...
body_text:
The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties.

In a statement sent to Al Jazeera on Monday, the Pentagon said the allegations were “baseless”.

“Any claim that the Deputy directed companies to use Goldman Sachs is categorically false. He worked with financial firms across the industry throughout his entire career,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in the statement.

“He has no favorites, and neither does the Department of War.”

The publication Bloomberg first reported the allegations, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg’s report, Feinberg guided defence contractors like Lockheed Martin and RTX towards working with Goldman Sachs banker Jim Donovan during their negotiations with the Pentagon.

Donovan and Feinberg reportedly knew each other. Bloomberg said Donovan has previously worked for the investment firm Feinberg co-founded, Cerberus Capital Management, which claims to oversee $70bn in assets.

Bloomberg’s report has raised concerns about a conflict of interest during the lucrative Pentagon negotiations.

Defence contracts are often million, if not billion, dollar deals. Guiding a company that is competing for a contract to work with a specific banker could be seen as a way of rigging the negotiations.

It would also put the banker in line to potentially receive large commissions from the contracts in question.

According to Bloomberg, both RTX and Lockheed Martin hired Donovan after Feinberg’s suggestion.

The Pentagon, however, has accused Bloomberg of seeking to lend credibility to unsubstantiated allegations.

“Despite the Department’s categorical denial, Bloomberg appears more interested in advancing a baseless smear than establishing the facts. Your sources are playing you, and Bloomberg should know better,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss told Al Jazeera.

“The Deputy is a man of honor and integrity. Unfortunately, some would rather see him fail than succeed.”

Feinberg was nominated by President Donald Trump for his position in one of the Pentagon’s top posts.

The Senate confirmed him in a vote of 59 to 40, and he was sworn in as the 36th deputy defense secretary on March 17, 2025, according to the Pentagon.

Lockheed Martin and RTX, both aerospace and defence companies, have longstanding ties to the Pentagon.

In August, for instance, the Department of Defense announced a multibillion-dollar deal with Lockheed Martin and another defence giant Northrop Grumman to boost production of parts for the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems.

According to Bloomberg’s reporting, Donovan, the banker, was a part of several deals in recent months involving Lockheed Martin and RTX.

They include a $59bn contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot missiles and two missile contracts worth approximately $45bn with RTX.

It is unclear who the anonymous sources for Bloomberg’s story might be.

Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has opened multiple investigations into leaks of sensitive information and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and other Pentagon resources.

title: David Jones’ total debt is over $400m including millions owed to staff, administrators confirm
excerpt:
Creditors meeting hears upmarket retailer owes $11m to employees and recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Upmarket retailer Da...
body_text:
Creditors meeting hears upmarket retailer owes $11m to employees and recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into administration earlier this month owing well over $400m, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol broke down the 188-year-old chain’s massive debt pile, including an estimated $180m owed to suppliers and $11m to employees.

There is also about $33m in unredeemed gift cards held by shoppers, which the retailer is still accepting, and significant sums owed to secured creditors including the retailer’s main financier, Hilco.

David Jones collapsed into voluntary administration in early November after years of steep losses left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent and supplier payments.

The retailer is set to shutter half of its 38 department stores by the end of the year, triggering mass job losses under a sweeping restructure.

Under a dual appointment, FTI Consulting has day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.

David Jones recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, according to updated figures disclosed to creditors. It lost a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.

Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.

Guardian Australia has reported that some suppliers are owed money from stock sent as early as April.

title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
excerpt:
Community leader says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quart...
body_text:
Community leader says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.

But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.

Theonila Roka Matbob, a former cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.

Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.

“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.

“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.

“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”

The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.

The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.

Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.

It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.

Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.

That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.

The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.

Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.

PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.

In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.

The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

title: Former USMNT coach says 'American sports reward losers' as he leaves for Manchester United
excerpt:
Lane Kiffin told us that LSU would be a school for the elites only, only for the program to miss the CFP playoffs in his first year leading the program.

Americans are used to dominating just about ev...
body_text:
Lane Kiffin told us that LSU would be a school for the elites only, only for the program to miss the CFP playoffs in his first year leading the program.

Americans are used to dominating just about every sport we care about, which makes our ongoing mediocrity in men’s soccer tough to swallow.

As former USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino heads to Manchester United after 26 months in charge, his takeaways from running U.S. soccer are a bad look for the program.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

United States Head Coach Mauricio Pochettino reacts to a call with the assistant referee during the international friendly match between the United States and Germany at Soldier Field in Chicago, Ill., on June 6, 2026. (Michael Miller/ISI Photos)

Coming from European football, trying to build a winner inside a system that cushions failure was a problem from day one. He summed up America's dilemma with soccer to Spanish newspaper El País during the 2026 World Cup.

"American sports reward losers," he said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Over in Europe, losing gets your club relegated and puts jobs on the line.

In Major League Soccer, nobody gets booted out of the league, and finishing in the cellar just gets you rewarded with a top draft pick. That setup completely kills the survival instinct you need to win at the highest level.

MAURICIO POCHETTINO TOLD USMNT PLAYERS 'WE'RE AMERICAN, WE DON'T TAKE S***' AHEAD OF WORLD CUP

"If you start in MLS and you haven’t won a game in three months and you’re at the bottom, what’s the consequence if there’s no promotion or relegation, no international competition? Pochettino said. "Soccer is different: if you reward those who don’t win, if you don’t have goals, you don’t fight. If I lose, what happens? Nothing. They just fire the coach."

American sports fans have been calling this out for years: U.S. soccer is overly corporate and flat-out soft when real trophies are on the line.

LA GALAXY COACH GREG VANNEY SAYS TEAM USA WAS 'TOO NAIVE,' EXPLAINS CHRISTIAN PULISIC'S STRUGGLES

Mauricio Pochettino, head coach of the United States men's soccer team, drinks water during a press conference in Los Angeles on June 11, 2026, ahead of the FIFA World Cup Group D match against Paraguay. (Alex Livesey/FIFA/Getty Images)

"Also, the American player is disciplined, but with a sense of complacency that isn’t good in soccer," he said. "It took us a year and a half to change that mentality."

Nowhere was that battle against complacency more obvious than how Pochettino handled Christian Pulisic.

LANDON DONOVAN JOINS CHRISTIAN PULISIC CRITICISM FOLLOWING USA'S WORLD CUP EXIT WITH HARSH OBSERVATION

After Pulisic decided to sit out the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup, where the U.S. watched Mexico win the title in the final, Pochettino refused to give his most talented player the captain’s armband. He rolled with veteran Tim Ream at the 2026 World Cup, then passed over Pulisic again in October in favor of Tyler Adams. Pulisic can take over a game when he’s locked in, but putting up zero goals at a World Cup after taking a voluntary summer off raises fair questions about whether America’s biggest star has the grit to actually lead.

Even while keeping things friendly with the American soccer press corps, he clearly got tired of coverage that graded the team on a soft curve instead of holding players to real international standards.

Christian Pulisic of the United States is consoled by Mauricio Pochettino, Head Coach of the United States, after being substituted during the FIFA World Cup 2026 Round of 16 match between USA and Belgium at Seattle Stadium on July 6, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (John Dorton/USSF/Getty Images)

Head coach Mauricio Pochettino of United States of America celebrates after a win in the FIFA World Cup 2026 Round of 32 match between United States of America and Bosnia and Herzegovina on July 1, 2026 at San Francisco Bay Area Stadium in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"I understand the culture of football," Pochettino insisted.

To be fair, Pochettino’s point only goes so far. America’s closed-league setup keeps franchises financially stable instead of letting clubs go bankrupt like they do in Europe, and the USMNT’s 4-1 Round of 16 loss to Belgium showed that a tougher attitude won’t close a talent gap overnight.

TEAM USA ISSUES STATEMENT IN ENGLISH AND SPANISH AFTER DISASTROUS WORLD CUP EXIT

As U.S. Soccer starts looking at potential successors like Steve Cherundolo, B.J. Callaghan, Pellegrino Matarazzo and former Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola, whom Pochettino recommended for the job.

Until U.S. soccer stops protecting players from failure, this program is going to stay an afterthought when the real heavyweights show up.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
excerpt: Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi ter...
body_text:
Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest.

Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks.

In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications.

He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts.

The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reported that the Houthis had cut off a key government supply route along the Red Sea coast, forcing troops to abandon several positions as concerns grew over a possible Houthi offensive towards Aden.

The military escalation coincided with a political development, as Yemen’s parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising their activities, financing and supply of weapons.

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the bill provides for prosecuting those involved in violations attributed to the group, freezing and confiscating affiliated assets, and imposing tougher penalties for offences, including attacks on civilians, planting landmines and targeting international shipping.

The legislation will now be submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, for enactment.

The latest developments come six weeks after government forces launched “Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, seeking to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.

title: Curt Cignetti fires back at Indiana 'easy' schedule critics: 'I really don't give a s---'
excerpt: "I have no idea how they put Indiana fourth. I have absolutely no idea. And I'm here for it. They must value a win in the Big House, I guess. I don't know, they must value playing Ohio State close, an...
body_text:
"I have no idea how they put Indiana fourth. I have absolutely no idea. And I'm here for it. They must value a win in the Big House, I guess. I don't know, they must value playing Ohio State close, and the only reason that I could see that Indiana is ahead of Ohio State is simply this: the quarterback for OSU."

Indiana Hoosiers head football coach Curt Cignetti doesn’t want to hear a peep about their strength of schedule compared to other College Football Playoff hopefuls.

Cignetti, whose team is 9-1 and 6-1 in Big Ten play, has remained at No. 6 in the AP Top 25 poll for the past five weeks, and is sitting at No. 9 in the CFP rankings.

The CFP committee will unveil another week of rankings on Tuesday, but the eight teams above Indiana all picked up wins like they did on Saturday, so there might not be much movement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Indiana Hoosiers head coach Curt Cignetti is seen following a college football game between the Northwestern Wildcats and Indiana Hoosiers on Sept. 25, 2026, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Either way, Cignetti was asked by a student reporter, Ian Plaskoff, on Monday during his news conference about his team’s conference record, and furthermore, how those teams have fared after facing them. In total, Indiana’s conference opponents are a combined 8-16, and Plaskoff believed it was indicative of how physical the Hoosiers can be rather than what the discourse has been about their schedule.

It is believed by some that Indiana has benefited from a weaker schedule not just this season, but in years past. In the last three years since Cignetti took over the program, they are 36-3.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Cignetti had time today to bash all those with that thinking.

"Well, you know, we don’t play anybody. We have a soft schedule, right?" he said. "That’s all I’ve heard around here for three years. People like to discredit us and what we’ve accomplished. … The good thing about it is, I think it feeds into our motivation and our chip. And that’s why I’m not afraid to keep it alive. And you know what? I’m 65 years old and I really don’t give a s---."

Cignetti acknowledged that his comments were going to only fuel the fire surrounding the Hoosiers’ "easy" schedule, but he didn’t care.

Indiana Hoosiers head coach Curt Cignetti walks onto the field before a college football game between the Michigan State Spartans and Indiana Hoosiers on Oct. 18, 2025, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

He went on to point out how Northwestern and Nebraska were both undefeated before playing them earlier this season. Their only blemish on the record was against Ohio State, who lost Julian Sayin during the game and hasn’t seen him return since.

Cignetti called it a "layup" that they missed in terms of losing to the Buckeyes, but their conference rival losing back-to-back games after beating them is being viewed as Indiana not facing a quality opponent in Ohio State.

"We ripped the heart out of that team," Cignetti said. "They haven’t been the same since without the quarterback. … We missed a layup."

Jul 22, 2025; Las Vegas, NV, USA; Indiana head coach Curt Cignetti speaks to the media during the Big Ten NCAA college football media days at Mandalay Bay Resort. (Lucas Peltier-Imagn Images)

Cignetti admitted, "You get tired of the narrative sometimes," but these are the reigning national champions. Yes, they are without their Heisman-winning quarterback, Fernando Mendoza, and many other key pieces of that undefeated squad from a season ago.
