title: Ukraine hits Putin's prized bridge in record drone blitz as Kremlin tells lawmakers to prepare for 'victory'
excerpt: The upcoming trilateral summit in China between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin faces critical global challenges. Alexandria Hoff reports on key agenda items, while retired Navy Captain...
body_text:
The upcoming trilateral summit in China between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin faces critical global challenges. Alexandria Hoff reports on key agenda items, while retired Navy Captain Brent Sadler analyzes strategic threats from Iran. Discussions are expected to address nuclear talks, international trade and the potential inclusion of tech leaders.

Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest overnight drone attack of the war Monday, striking President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge and setting industrial facilities ablaze, as separate reports revealed a covert French military mission in Ukraine and preparations in Moscow for a possible return of Russian troops.

The developments came days before President Donald Trump is expected to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, amid renewed U.S.-brokered efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.

"The sheer scale and effectiveness of these drone attacks are remarkable," retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital. "Ukraine has developed the capability to produce large numbers of drones and strike targets once considered a safe haven deep inside Russia."

UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS

Flames engulf industrial structures as a massive fire lights up the night sky in Nizhnekamsk, Russia, Nov. 15, 2026. (Reuters)

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, exceeding the previous overnight record of 1,254 on Oct. 29, Reuters reported Nov. 16. The numbers could not be independently verified.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones had been launched toward the capital region since Sunday evening, with 191 intercepted.

Russian-installed Crimean governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed that the Kerch Strait bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia, had been struck. The Kremlin characterized the damage as minor. Road traffic was temporarily suspended for repairs, while trains continued running, according to Russian transportation officials.

The bridge is both a strategically important supply route and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The strikes also hit Russia's energy sector. Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar reported fires at four industrial sites in Azov, where three people were injured. Officials in neighboring Krasnodar said a separate fire broke out at an industrial facility in Ilsky. Falling drone debris reportedly injured six people in the Krasnodar region.

ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE

Rescuers from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine work at a packaging facility damaged by a Russian attack in Odesa region, Ukraine, on November 16, 2026. The strike destroyed a two-storey administrative and warehouse building, damaged the roof of a production facility and shattered windows. Two people were injured in the attack. (Nina Liashonok/Ukrinform via Reuters)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Sunday that strikes had disabled more than half of Russia's refining capacity, a figure Fox News Digital could not verify. Two industry sources separately estimated that recent attacks reduced refining capacity by approximately 30%, Reuters reported.

"Putin has a serious problem on his hands," Newton said. "Russia is enormous in terms of size; there’s simply no way to 100% defend every refinery, airfield, and military installation."

Newton said Ukraine's campaign was designed to strengthen its negotiating position while disrupting Russia's military and logistics networks.

"I don’t believe Ukraine has reached a culminating point yet, by any stretch, to change Putin’s mind, but sustained military and economic pressure just may eventually at some point force him to reconsider his position," he said.

In a separate development, Radio France Internationale reported Nov. 16 that French troops had been operating inside Ukraine since at least summer 2026 as part of a confidential mission codenamed "Volia."

The mission reportedly consists of small teams making short visits to train Ukrainian personnel and maintain equipment. RFI said French lawmakers had not been informed and alleged that an established French training operation in Poland, known as "Gerfaut," provided a gateway for deployments into Ukraine.

An anonymous source familiar with the mission confirmed French personnel's presence to AFP, while stressing that they were not combat troops.

"The rotation of French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine is a reality," the source told AFP. "But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions."

France's military general staff did not immediately comment to AFP. The number of troops involved remains unknown.

Smoke and flames rise over Moscow on June 18, 2026, following a Ukrainian drone attack that hit the Kapotnya oil refinery and other targets in the Russian capital. (East2West)

Meanwhile, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported Nov. 16 that Kremlin officials had instructed lawmakers from Putin's United Russia party to prepare for "victory" and the return of personnel from the battlefield.

The message was reportedly delivered during a closed-door seminar attended by senior presidential administration official Sergei Kiriyenko. A source described lawmakers being told to anticipate the possibility of soldiers returning home simultaneously.

The report provided no timetable and did not establish that Putin had ordered a withdrawal or decided to end the war.

The reports emerged after U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi last week resulted in a major prisoner-exchange agreement but no breakthrough over territory.

Trump, Putin and Xi were due to meet Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China, with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov describing the trilateral summit as a potentially significant event.

Newton expressed skepticism about an immediate diplomatic breakthrough. "I don't anticipate a major breakthrough on any issue, including Russia's war against Ukraine," he said.

Left to right: Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (Reuters)

"If President Trump has any discussions with Xi and Putin regarding Ukraine I would advise him to look those two leaders in the eye and underscore the U.S. is not backing down in our support to the Ukrainian people as they valiantly defend their homeland," he concluded.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Third US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East as Iran rules out UN nuclear inspections
excerpt: Stakes rise as President Donald Trump prepares for his Asia trip to hold trilateral talks on Thursday. Christian Whiton analyzes the geopolitical implications alongside reports of Jensen Huang weighin...
body_text:
Stakes rise as President Donald Trump prepares for his Asia trip to hold trilateral talks on Thursday. Christian Whiton analyzes the geopolitical implications alongside reports of Jensen Huang weighing an Nvidia comeback 33 years after founding the company.

The USS Roosevelt aircraft carrier on Sunday reportedly entered the region overseen by U.S. Central Command, which means that the American military now has three carriers positioned in the region again.

"The USS Roosevelt aircraft carrier has arrived in the U.S. military central command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility earlier on Sunday, a U.S. official tells me," Israeli journalist Barak Ravid wrote in a Sunday post on X. "The U.S. military now has three air craft carrier strike groups in CENTCOM."

The Pentagon referred Fox News Digital to CENTCOM, which did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Monday.

IRAN VOWS 'WE WILL FIND YOU' TO 2 US NAVY OFFICERS THE DAY WARSHIP RETURNS FROM MIDDLE EAST

An EA-18G Growler assigned to Electric Attack Squadron (VAQ) 137 lands aboard the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) while the ship is moored in Honolulu, Hawaii, during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 on July 17, 2026. (Michelle Bir / AFP via Getty Images)

The news comes as the U.S.-Iran war continues more than eight months after it began earlier this year.

There were previously three carriers positioned in the region earlier this year, as CENTCOM noted in April.

BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS

A flight deck director signals an F-35C Lightning II on the flight deck aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 while underway in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on July 17, 2026. (Michelle Bir / AFP via Getty Images)

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi has reportedly indicated that the nation will not grant the International Atomic Energy Agency access to facilities until the war has concluded.

"We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran's conditions are met and the war has permanently ended," he said, according to CBS News.

DHS CHIEF MULLIN SAYS IRAN POSES DAILY THREAT TO TRUMP AND HIS FAMILY AMID DRONE CONCERNS

A Persian-to-English translation from material on Iran's irib-news.ir website indicates that Gharibabadi said that "our current policy with the Agency is that as long as this situation is not resolved, the talk of war is not permanently ended, a diplomatic understanding is not established, and the United States does not establish its own interactions, we cannot establish access to the Agency."

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Why Starshield limits are hurting Ukraine against jet-powered drones
excerpt: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort a...
body_text:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia.

Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity.

Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.

Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX  to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas.

In a statement on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other.

He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”.

“We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added.

Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days.

This is not the first time Ukrainian officials have complained about limits on Starshield hampering Kyiv’s defence efforts.

Last month, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian missile and drone strikes, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.

According to a November 2 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Starshield is critical to Ukraine since it helps in encrypting satellite communications, which are needed to guide drones in order to carry out interceptions.

“In addition to using Starshield service for strikes within Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, Ukraine uses Starshield-equipped drones to intercept and defend against Russian drones, such as new jet-powered drones taking aim at Ukrainian critical infrastructure and civilian targets,” the CSIS report noted.

Without access to Starshield internet, these Ukrainian drones are unable to work as effectively.

“Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered ‘shaheds’,” Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday.

After last month’s disruptions, Zelenskyy said on X that “intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.

“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he added.

Last month, Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, had posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (161km/h).

That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he had said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.

Officials have said the restrictions have also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

Jet-powered drones are high-speed uncrewed aerial vehicles equipped with small turbojet engines rather than traditional propellers or piston engines.

In its war on Ukraine, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered variants such as the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 models.

These drones fly at much higher speeds than traditional propeller-powered drones, making them significantly harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept.

In August, 38 people were killed in the village of Myla in Ukraine, when a Russian drone attack struck an ammunition depot. Another 12 were killed in attacks across the country in September.

Ukraine’s Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said in September that while the country has an interception rate of more than 90 percent against propeller-powered drones, that success rate falls to only 60 percent against jet-powered models.

Ukraine has, however, retaliated using its own drone systems, and has also struck Russian refineries, hitting 12 in August, along with two gas-processing plants and three oil shipment terminals, according to its defence ministry.

On Sunday, Ukraine’s army said it also shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

But to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones more efficiently, Zelenskyy said he had told teams of Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and the presidential office “to work as closely as possible with the American side and SpaceX” and remove restrictions on Starshield.

“It is important to be on the right side of history. It is essential to help Ukraine,” he said on Sunday.

Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, is yet to respond to recent accusations about Starshield from Zelenskyy.

But last month, the company and Musk denied restricting internet speeds.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote last month, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.

Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times last month that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.

The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.

Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Donald Trump returned to the presidency last year, including over Washington’s increasing reluctance to militarily support Ukraine and its mounting efforts to forge a deal with Russia.

But Trump has said that it is Musk who controls Starlink’s operations in Ukraine.

When asked about internet restrictions in Ukraine, he told reporters last month that Musk had restored Kyiv’s access, while denying any White House role in the episode.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said last month that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠⁠⁠⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio had said.

Meanwhile, officials from Ukraine and Russia held peace talks in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, last week. The talks, mediated by the US, only yielded an agreement on a prisoner exchange and failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark.

The US, however, pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join NATO, an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia.

According to Zelenskyy, Trump’s administration has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.

But Zelenskyy said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.

The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal. But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.

Moscow has, however, insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.

title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
excerpt:
The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)

Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, i...
body_text:
The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)

Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

title: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
excerpt:
The Estonian government says it will shut the crossings after accusing Russia of directing an alleged sabotage attack on a drone manufacturer

Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russ...
body_text:
The Estonian government says it will shut the crossings after accusing Russia of directing an alleged sabotage attack on a drone manufacturer

Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".

The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.

They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.

On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.

The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.

Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.

The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.

Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.

One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.

Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."

Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.

Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.

Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

title: ‘My arms are empty’: Tragedy strikes Gaza family after baby dies from cold
excerpt: Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For Susan Arqiq, the hardest part of the day comes at night, when the noise around her fades and she is left alone with the absence of her nine-month-old son, Kinan. She is s...
body_text:
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For Susan Arqiq, the hardest part of the day comes at night, when the noise around her fades and she is left alone with the absence of her nine-month-old son, Kinan. She is still struggling to understand how the cold took his life.

Susan, 26, had put him to sleep beside her on Wednesday night, as she had done countless times before, at their camp in Khan Younis. When she woke in the early hours of the morning to change his diaper, she found Kinan’s face blue, his hands stiff and his body cold.

Her arms, which had held him through countless nights, are now empty.

“My son was pressed against the tent’s tarpaulin. The bedding was still damp,” she told Al Jazeera.

“I switched on my phone’s flashlight and found that his face was completely blue, his hands were stiff, and his body was like ice. My heart nearly stopped from fear. I immediately woke my husband. I was screaming, ‘Kinan, Kinan!’ I could not understand what was wrong with him.”

Her husband did not speak. He picked up the baby and, accompanied by men from the camp, rushed him to hospital.

Women from neighbouring tents, woken by the cries, gathered around Susan. They tried to reassure her that her baby would be all right, but the news from the hospital confirmed her fears.

Kinan died on Thursday, November 12, after a severe drop in his body temperature, according to medical sources. His death was the first cold-related fatality recorded in Gaza during the current winter season.

Susan and her husband, Ahmed Arqiq, 33, have been in shock since the tragic death of their son. Ahmed says Kinan had no known health problems before that night.

“At the emergency department, they told me, ‘May God compensate you. The child has died, and the cause is the severe drop in temperature,’” Ahmed says. “I was shocked… My heart is broken, and even now I cannot believe it.”

Israel’s war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, has seen at least 73,600 Palestinians killed and large parts of the occupied Palestinian territory reduced to rubble. Due to the destruction of their homes or Israeli military occupation, around 1.4 million people are living in tents or makeshift displacement camps.

Israel’s siege on Gaza has prevented mobile homes, tarpaulins, and other essential materials from entering the territory.

The Arqiq family are one of many living in a worn-out displacement tent in the al-Mawasi camp near Khan Younis in southern Gaza as winter approaches. The shelter offers little protection from the cold or the rain, which flooded camps across Gaza during a storm last week.

Ahmed has been unable to find work since the war, and they struggle to afford even the basic necessities of life.

“I have struggled to obtain adequate shelter, blankets, clothing and food for my children. My life is all about suffering,” he said. “Look at my tent. We live in poor conditions. During the last winter storm, we were flooded with water.”

Ahmed said the family had not received a proper tent or tarpaulin to protect them from the winter weather before Kinan’s death. After Kinan died, they received the waterproof sheet, but it was too late to protect him.

Kinan was the youngest of three children, and his brothers, Rami, three, and Ali, two, were deeply attached to him. They continue to ask about their younger brother, unable to understand why he is no longer with them.

“They always ask where he has gone. Whenever they see his belongings, they try to look for him. It is unbelievable,” Ahmed said.

Kinan’s death has renewed fears among displaced families in Gaza as winter sets in. Last week, heavy rain and flooding battered displacement camps across Gaza, damaging tents and leaving families exposed to cold and wet conditions. At least four children died in the floods.

Babies are particularly vulnerable to hypothermia as their bodies are less able to regulate temperature, especially when exposed to cold for prolonged periods.

At least 11 babies are believed to have died due to the cold in Gaza last winter.

Hadeel al-Midana, 27, lives in a displacement tent west of Gaza City with her three children: Hamza and his two older brothers, Mahmoud, seven, and Nour al-Din, five. Her husband, Ibrahim, has been out of work since the war.

She said Kinan’s death has deepened fears she carries each night when she tries to keep her own youngest son, one-month-old Hamza, warm.

“I am always on edge. I cannot leave him,” she told Al Jazeera.

The family struggles to keep the children warm with limited clothing and blankets.

“I swear, he doesn’t have a blanket of his own. I wrap him in the blankets that I use myself,” Hadeel says, referring to Hamza.

The family has received second-hand clothes from neighbours. They were also provided with four blankets at the camp, but Hadeel said the cold inside their tent remains difficult to endure.

“Even the adults cannot bear it. How much worse is it for the little children?” she asked.

She wakes up several times during the night to check on Hamza. Two nights ago, she found his hands and feet were as cold as ice. Terrified, she covered him with a thicker blanket.

She says she needs more blankets for her baby and a small bed to lift him off the ground.

“I need blankets for him, and perhaps a bed that would raise him a little above the ground. I am afraid of the insects, too,” she said.

“The tent is not fit for a child’s life, or even an adult’s life. We live in constant fear, and there is nothing we can do to face it. I hope we get through this winter safely.”

title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
excerpt:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year

US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief...
body_text:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year

US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.

But now fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.

"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.

The Trump administration issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres on Monday, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models ahead of Trump's meeting with China President Xi Jingping.

The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.

The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

FOX News Media will present the "All American Christmas Tree Lighting" on Friday, November 20, during a special edition of "The Five" at 5 p.m. ET.

The seventh annual "All American Christmas Tree Lighting," sponsored by Ace Hardware, will be hosted by Emily Compagno, Harold Ford Jr., Greg Gutfeld, Dana Perino and Jesse Watters, who will light the tree outside the network’s New York City headquarters.

First lady Melania Trump will attend the event and join children for a festive Christmas celebration in a winter wonderland filled with holiday cheer.

The first lady will help decorate a Christmas tree, enjoy cookies and hot chocolate with the children, and share favorite holiday traditions and Christmas wish lists.

Dana Perino and Greg Gutfeld speak at the 6th Annual "All-American Christmas Tree Lighting" at Fox News Channel Studios on Nov. 21, 2025, in New York City. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)

title: Widely used antidepressant outperformed by 3 other drugs in major study of 30,000 people
excerpt: Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed ...
body_text:
Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed foods.

Three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine, widely known by the brand name Prozac, at helping people with depression get better and stay well over time, a new study suggests.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, compared 20 antidepressants to determine how well they eased depression symptoms and helped prevent them from returning over time.

Researchers analyzed 115 previous clinical trials involving more than 30,000 people, according to a news release from Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands.

CERTAIN SLEEP HABITS COULD OFFER CLUES TO HIDDEN TYPE OF DEPRESSION, SCIENTISTS SAY

They found that escitalopram, sold under the brand name Lexapro; duloxetine, sold as Cymbalta; and agomelatine performed better over the long term than fluoxetine, which researchers used as the main comparison drug.

Eli Lilly told Fox News Digital that it discontinued manufacturing Prozac in 2024. The company noted that fluoxetine remains available in many FDA-approved generic medicines and that neither the study nor the university’s news release specifically referred to Prozac or any Lilly product.

A new study suggests three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine at helping people recover from depression and stay well over time. (iStock)

The findings suggest that antidepressants can continue helping people after their symptoms improve, although some medications appeared to work better than others at keeping patients well.

Paul van Haaren, a researcher at Radboud University Medical Center who worked on the study, noted that the three medications have different benefits and drawbacks.

"Escitalopram is already widely used," he said in the release. "Agomelatine works well, but one of its side effects is the risk of liver failure. Duloxetine is less well-known and is prescribed less frequently as a first-line treatment."

Escitalopram belongs to a common group of antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications are often recommended as a first option for treating depression, according to the release.

Researchers compared antidepressant treatments to better understand which medications may help patients maintain improvements and avoid a return of depression symptoms. (iStock)

Among the SSRIs included in the study, escitalopram appeared to work best at helping patients stay well over time.

Eric Ruhé, a professor of difficult-to-treat depression at Radboud University Medical Center, said the findings could eventually influence how doctors choose antidepressants. Still, the researchers stressed that this does not mean everyone with depression should take escitalopram.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"As a prescriber, you consider the balance between a medication's benefits and side effects," Ruhé said in the release. "That balance differs from person to person."

Dr. Carole Lieberman, a board-certified psychiatrist based in Beverly Hills, California, who was not involved in the study, urged caution when interpreting the findings.

Escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine appeared to outperform fluoxetine in maintaining improvements in depression symptoms over the long term. (iStock)

She noted that agomelatine is not approved in the U.S.

"The best way to treat someone with depression is not always with antidepressants, and certainly not with antidepressants alone," Lieberman told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Psychotherapy or talk therapy can also play an important role in treating depression, according to Lieberman, while some patients may benefit from using medication along with therapy.

There were some limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged.

Researchers cautioned that the findings cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific patient, emphasizing the need for individualized treatment decisions. (iStock)

Rather than enrolling a new group of patients and following them over time, the researchers combined results from 115 previous clinical trials to compare how the medications performed.

The findings also cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific person. The researchers stressed that doctors and patients should consider both the potential benefits and side effects when choosing a medication.

People with questions about their antidepressants should speak with their doctor before making any medication changes, according to the release.

Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers and additional drug manufacturers for comment.

Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

title: ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows
excerpt:
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a protest, her attorney says

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US...
body_text:
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a protest, her attorney says

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.

Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she is part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area.

A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows.

Footage filmed by Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera, captured a tumultuous scene as several people protested the agents making the arrest. The circumstances of the man’s arrest were not immediately clear, and he has not been identified. Agents wore law enforcement vests and ICE badges, and at least two of them had masks covering their faces.

It was unclear what exactly happened right before Vargas Andrade’s arrest, with the sound on the footage repeatedly cutting out. One woman was heard screaming at the agents to get away from her and another cursed at the agents, telling them, “You should be embarrassed … you guys are so fucked up.”

Vargas Andrade had her phone in one hand as she and an agent then appeared to bump into each other, footage showed. That agent then grabbed her and started to handcuff her. Another agent then pulled out what appeared to be a pepper-spray canister and pointed it at the direction of Vargas Andrade and her husband who was filming.

The footage partially captured the agent deploying the pepper spray, though it was difficult to discern how long he sprayed it and where the chemicals landed. Soon after, the footage captured Talavera shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents moved to detain his wife. Seconds later, two agents took Vargas Andrade to the ground where she was handcuffed on her stomach with her hands behind her back, before one of the agents moved her onto her side.

Vargas Andrade was taken into custody and transported to an ICE field office in Stockton, according to her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski. Vargas Andrade’s sister had called for an ambulance, which then arrived at the ICE facility and transported her to a hospital, her family and a local advocate said at the press conference.

Vargas Andrade said officers had told her she was accused of assaulting an ICE agent, an accusation she denied. She was released later that day, and she has not been charged with any crimes, according to Kolasinski.

Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Monday. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice (DoJ) declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Stanislaus sheriff’s office, which runs the jail, said sheriff deputies were not involved in Vargas Andrade’s arrest.

“They threw me to the ground, they maced me, then they handcuffed me,” Vargas Andrade recalled to reporters on Sunday night. “I told the ICE agent … ‘I’m pregnant, so don’t put your hands on me.’ … They right away threw me on the floor … I was burning. I couldn’t breathe. The mace went up my nose.”

Another ICE agent then gave her water to wash her face, she recalled.

“I got scared,” Talavera said. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”

Vargas Andrade said she was particularly worried because she had suffered two previous pregnancy losses, but she said doctors did an ultrasound after the incident and did not identify any concerns.

The encounter happened amid reports of increased ICE activity in California’s central valley region, which is home to the state’s agricultural industry. DHS and the justice department have repeatedly accused anti-ICE protesters of assaulting agents, though many of those prosecutions in California have fallen apart in federal court.

“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

title: Devon police allowed known abuser who shot his wife to have shotguns
excerpt:
Ex-marine John Perkins, who also killed himself, had been repeatedly violent to Kathryn Perkins over 42-year marriage, Exeter inquests hear

A “controlling and violent” former Royal Marine who shot hi...
body_text:
Ex-marine John Perkins, who also killed himself, had been repeatedly violent to Kathryn Perkins over 42-year marriage, Exeter inquests hear

A “controlling and violent” former Royal Marine who shot his wife dead after she told him she was leaving was allowed to keep two licensed shotguns despite police knowing he had a history of domestic abuse.

John Perkins shot Kathryn Perkins at their home in Devon with a double-barrelled shotgun before killing himself with his second weapon.

The couple’s inquests in Exeter were told that Perkins, 66, had repeatedly been violent towards Kathryn Perkins, 67, during their 42-year-old marriage, beginning when he head-butted her during their honeymoon.

The coroner, Alison Longhorn, area coroner for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay, concluded that Kathryn Perkins had been unlawfully killed and John Perkins killed himself.

Perkins’ violence towards his wife and his anger issues were recorded in his medical records and passed to Devon and Cornwall police when Perkins applied for his shotgun licence to be renewed.

Even so, police approved his application and Perkins was allowed to keep his shotguns, which he said he wanted for pheasant and deer shooting.

Longhorn said she was concerned that when someone applied for a shotgun licence, the scrutiny of any history of domestic abuse did not appear as “thorough, considered or as carefully and accurately documented as it should be”. She said she would write to Devon and Cornwall police and the Home Office about the case.

The relationship continued to deteriorate and shortly before he shot his wife in May 2025 Perkins searched the internet to find out if it was possible to get a silencer for a shotgun.

Devon and Cornwall police’s handling of firearms applications came under intense scrutiny for allowing Jake Davison to have the pump action shotgun he used to kill five people in Plymouth in 2021.

In a statement read out at the inquest, the couple’s son, Bradley Perkins, described his father as violent, controlling and unpredictable.

He said that when he was 11, his father punched him in the face, leaving him with a black eye and prompting social services to become involved. He also spoke about a time when Perkins punched his wife in the head as they drove home from a ski trip.

By May 2025, Bradley Perkins said his mother had decided to leave her husband and went to their house in Exmouth, Devon, to tell him.

Bradley Perkins said when he failed to hear from his mother, he went to their home and found his parents’ bodies. “I was screaming and could not believe what I was seeing,” he said.

Kathryn Perkins’ sister, Barbara, described Perkins as a bully and an “egotistical narcissist” who had head-butted his wife on their honeymoon.

She said her sister had contacted domestic abuse support at one point and that in 2010 John Perkins had attended an NHS anger management course but did not complete it because he thought it was “rubbish”.

The inquest was told that Perkins’ medical records recorded that he was referred on to the course because he had “smacked” his wife.

Police were told about this by Perkins’ GP when he asked for his firearms licence to be renewed in 2023.

An experienced officer was sent to the couple’s address and spoke to Kathryn Perkins but she said she had no concerns about her husband having shotguns.

Police also knew that in 1995 Perkins had had an altercation with a neighbour but this was disregarded as irrelevant.

Devon and Cornwall police told the inquest changes were being made to how licensing applications were considered when concerns about domestic violence were raised but they had not yet been completed.

title: Beer-drinking, cigarette-smoking 87-year-old viral Internet golfer 'Par 3 Lee' drains another ace
excerpt:
Lane Kiffin told us that LSU would be a school for the elites only, only for the program to miss the CFP playoffs in his first year leading the program.

It took Lee McFarlane 46 years to get his seco...
body_text:
Lane Kiffin told us that LSU would be a school for the elites only, only for the program to miss the CFP playoffs in his first year leading the program.

It took Lee McFarlane 46 years to get his second hole-in-one. It took him just 141 days to get his third.

The 87-year-old Toledo, Ohio retiree — who became an overnight folk hero over the summer after a photo of him celebrating his second ace with a beer and a cigarette in his hand went viral around the golf world — is back at it again. The 5-foot-5, 107-pound legend known around northwest Ohio as "Par Three Lee" (P3L) drained a hole-in-one last week at Ottawa Park Golf Course in Toledo, for his second ace this golf season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"I really didn't see it go in," P3L told OutKick of the tee shot with an 8-iron from 83 yards out. "I teed off first. I knew I was on the green, you know, and we were playing scrambles, so that's my job, is to get us on the green where we've got a chance. So I just hit the shot and turned around and started putting my club back in the bag, and [a scramble partner] said, 'Christ, I think this one went in!'" the 15-handicapper added.

The golf gods had struck again for a guy who says the sport has been a "godsend" since the death of his wife. "It gets me out of the house. I forget about everything that's going on around the house and with the family, and with all my friends on the golf course, and it's been my life," he continued.

"I tell most of the guys I played with are and they're late 50s, 60s, and 70s or old, you know, 15, 20 years younger than I am. But I keep telling them, you stay on the golf course, or you bowl or you do something active to keep going, because that's what keeps your body alive."

WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS

How much golf is this guy playing? We're talking over 100 rounds per summer. He's playing five times a week in Ohio during the summer season. That's not counting an annual blowout golf trip with 54 guys that he's a regular on. There's a trip to Alabama to visit his son to play Robert Trent Jones courses.

What about indoor golf? "No, I do not like indoor golf," a defiant P3L fired back. "I have tried it three times, and the screens just do not read the balls correctly. When they hit the screen, you can hit one chip and it'll go 35 yards, and the next one goes 70 yards."

Toledo, Ohio golfer Par 3 Lee, 87, became an Internet superstar in June after posing with a beer and a cig after draining his second career hole in one. Last week, he made another ace. (Chippewa Golf Club / User submitted)

While the YouTube golf world is busy praising participants in the Internet Invitational and yelling from the rooftop about how they're growing the game, Par Three Lee just goes about his business influencing the sport the only way he knows how: By playing solid golf, sucking down cold beers and smoking his cigs like it's his retirement job, because it is.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The results of Lee's influencing speak for themselves.

Nearly 34k people 'Liked' Instagram golf page Zire Golf's post in June celebrating Par Three Lee's iconic pose after is second hole in one. The comment section realized the hero that the golf gods had sent us:

Life goals, Man. We should all be so fortunate to still be out there teeing it up at 87. Well done!

AMERICA'S BIGGEST BEER-LOVING STATES REVEALED — SEE WHERE YOURS RANKS

Has all this fame gone to P3L's head? Absolutely not. He hasn't forgotten the little guys, especially after making national news with his aces. "The one I had at [Chippewa], there was 28 of us playing that day, so my bar tab was a little higher. [Last week], I had to buy eight beers—and one guy doesn't drink at all," Lee said of his financial well-being after paying up with free beers for his buddies.

What's his standard budget before hole-in-one beers?

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"I'll spend $25 in greens fees, put $10 in the prize kitty, and then spend $25 on beer afterwards," P3L noted.

What would it take for an Internet writer and a couple of buddies to get Lee as a hole-in-one hunter for our scramble team?

"Just ask. I'll probably buy you a beer whether I make a hole-in-one or not."

Joe Kinsey is the Senior Director of Content of OutKick.

title: Senate Dem challenging Sen Chuck Schumer for leadership post backs Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker
excerpt: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on the Democratic Party's internal leadership struggle as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, including growing suppor...
body_text:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on the Democratic Party's internal leadership struggle as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, including growing support for Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., as a potential challenger to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Pergram examines the divisions within the party, pressure for new leadership and what a potential shake-up could mean for Democrats' legislative agenda and political strategy on 'America Reports.'

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is currently challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the Senate Majority Leader role, has backed current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., in his bid for the speaker's gavel.

Asked by Politico's Will Steakin whether he supports Jeffries for the post, Van Hollen said that he does.

The senator noted that Jeffries has "been the minority leader, but he's not served as speaker before," adding that he thinks the congressman "should be given an opportunity to bring the caucus, uh, together in this moment."

CHRIS VAN HOLLEN FLOATS USING GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN THREAT TO FORCE TRUMP TO END IRAN WAR

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during the What's Next conference in Denver, Colo., on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Van Hollen's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Monday.

Schumer, the current Senate Minority Leader, is aiming to retain his party's leadership position next year when the Democrats will be in the majority. Last week, Van Hollen threw his hat into the ring to challenge Schumer for the post.

SEN BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS CHRIS VAN HOLLEN'S BID TO CHALLENGE SCHUMER FOR SENATE DEMOCRATIC LEADER POST

U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., arrives to the U.S. Capitol Building on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Schumer, who has been a senator since 1999, has been either the Senate minority or majority leader since 2017, which is the entire time that Van Hollen, who took office in 2017, has been serving in the Senate.

SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

So far, no House Democrats have launched a bid to compete with Jeffries for the House speakership.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump defends commerce secretary Lutnick for allegedly slow-walking Nvidia chip export restrictions – live
excerpt:
President backs Lutnick after treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed commerce department for delays in blocking advance AI chip exports

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutni...
body_text:
President backs Lutnick after treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed commerce department for delays in blocking advance AI chip exports

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick today, after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was ousted from his role following a revelation that he had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese operation.

Lutnick is now set to testify before Congress about delays by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.

Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said.

Lutnick is currently traveling with the president and other senior officials and cabinet members to Manila.

Meanwhile, Scott Bessent, Trump’s treasury secretary, said that he has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, in an interview with CNBC last week.

“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added on Friday.

As the leadership battle for Senate majority leader heats up between progressive Democrat Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer, the current minority leader, we’re watching for more on how the two are securing support of the wider caucus.

While several Democrats have said they don’t intend to back Schumer, they haven’t necessarily pledged to support Van Hollen.

Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek, who flipped Iowa’s open seat in the recent midterms, told reporters today that he’d spoken to both lawmakers but is still waiting for “further plans” from them about how they will deal with affordability in the US.

“I like both,” Turek added. “I have not given my allegiance to any leadership or any party, and I told Iowans I was going to sit down with them and say: ‘What are you going to do for Iowa?’”

As Donald Trump and tech leaders clamor for his return as Nvidia’s CEO, the company’s board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang.

The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, CNBC reports this morning, citing a person familiar with the matter. Reuters hears the same, also citing a person familiar.

Huang resigned on Thursday after reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

Elon Musk and other tech bosses have called for Huang’s reinstatement, amid reports the AI figurehead is already plotting a return to the chip company, just days after he was ousted. An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Here’s Trump expressing his support for the return of Huang and saying he “would not mind” him being reinstated.

The secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.

This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.

But this month, for the first time in recent memory, the island backed a Democrat for governor, casting 14 of their 21 votes for governor Josh Green and lieutenant governor Derek Kawakami. Has Ni‘ihau been caught up in the blue tsunami?

Donald Trump’s efforts to blame Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage – and the resulting travel chaos – on Democrats are “absurd”, an incoming Democratic member of Congress said yesterday.

The president remained largely silent and out of public view as air travel shut down on Friday, but yesterday he emerged to issue a series of posts blaming the incident on the Biden administration, despite Trump being in office for the last two years in which time Republicans have had control of Congress. He has continued this blame game today (see our earlier post).

Dan Koh, a US House representative-elect from Massachusetts and former Biden administration official, blasted the effort to cast aside blame.

“It’s kind of revisionist history – you might as well start blaming Ronald Reagan for the FAA strike in the 80s as part of this, too,” he said yesterday during an appearance on MS NOW’s The Weekend. “It’s absurd.”

Koh said Joe Biden secured “historic funding not only to the FAA but over a trillion dollars of infrastructure money” between Trump’s two presidencies. But, Koh added, “a lot of it … Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke”, invoking a term that those on the political right use to refer to things they perceive to be overly leftist.

The congressman-elect said he talks frequently with mayors and city council members in his district about “all this money that would help them with upgrades to transportation including flights” – but “they don’t even know if they’re going to get any more because the [Trump] administration has not even gotten back to them on the status.” He added:

double quotation markThis is the reality: Donald Trump likes to say it’s Biden’s fault, but it’s actually his policies that are stopping the funding from hitting the towns and cities.

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced on Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years from civil rights groups who have accused the unit of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters.

In a video released on Monday morning, Mamdani said the move stemmed from a campaign pledge he made to disband the New York City police department’s strategic response group (SRG). “Today, we are keeping that promise,” Mamdani said in the video.

An accompanying joint statement from Mamdani and NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch said the overhaul would “transform how the city prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest”.

Along with eliminating the SRG, which was founded in 2015 ostensibly to focus on counter-terrorism, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement also said that the city planned to establish a “first-of-its-kind, civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD)” within the mayor’s office of community safety.

That division will not have weapons or arrest powers, unlike the SRG, according to the announcement.

The city will also establish what they described as a “specialized dialogue team” that will be known as the “First Amendment Support Team” (Fast) within the NYPD’s community affairs bureau, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement said. The creation of Fast is meant to “improve the NYPD’s protest response”, and it will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation, the mayor and police commissioner said.

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick today, after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was ousted from his role following a revelation that he had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese operation.

Lutnick is now set to testify before Congress about delays by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.

Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said.

Lutnick is currently traveling with the president and other senior officials and cabinet members to Manila.

Meanwhile, Scott Bessent, Trump’s treasury secretary, said that he has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, in an interview with CNBC last week.

“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added on Friday.

Trump also continued to shift responsibility to Joe Biden administration for the national ground stop over the weekend, that saw thousands of flights.

This is just the second nationwide ​ground stop of all departures since the 9/11 attacks. The previous one came in January 2023, when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours.

“I hate to blame anybody, but the Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass, and if you know anything about electrical engineering you cannot hook up copper into glass,” Trump claimed. “A lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old, in some cases more than 50 years old, and we essentially want to blow it up and put a new one in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. So that’s what we’re doing, but we need the funding to get it done. But essentially what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.”

Trump’s claims comes after Congress, under Republican control, passed a $12.5bn air traffic control package in 2025, as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The president, however, appeared convinced that lawmakers would be now more willing to allocate more funding to upgrade the systems. “I think the one good thing that comes out of it I’m sure Congress now will give us the money,” he told reporters today.

Over the weekend, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said in an interview with ABC News that the existing funding did not provide money for “a new architecture for telecom”.

“I don’t have any money given by Congress to build a new software system to manage the airspace. They’re very specific on how we spend the 12.5 and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build,” he said.

However, the top House Democrats on two key transportation and aviation committees said in a statement that, as of now, $8bn remains unobligated and $11bn is unspent.

Today, Trump also scolded a reporter for questioning why he has spent considerable time devoting energy and resources to White House renovation projects, instead of the FAA upgrades.

“You’re so pathetic,” he said. “I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape, and it takes me 10 minutes a day. Very little time … That building, if you looked a year ago when I came back, was in horrible condition.”

Donald ⁠Trump said today that he ⁠would ​not ‌mind ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia.

Trump is speaking to reporters now, ahead of his trip to Manila to attend the Asean summit.

The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denies that national security has been put at risk.

“I think having Jensen go back – a lot of people are asking Jensen - they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” the president said.

That’s quite an intervention, as an open letter circulates calling for the chip giant to reinstate Huang.

Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.

An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.

One quick note on the US Senate race in Alaska. According to the state’s election laws, if no candidate manages to cross the 50% threshold, that triggers a ranked-choice runoff where the candidate with fewest votes is eliminated but their vote goes to their second choice (which they mark on their ballot). This happens in rounds until the candidate with the most votes wins.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington, before traveling to Manila, Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Trump’s first order or business will be his first meeting with the “Quad” alliance since he returned to the White House last year. This group includes Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, and Sanae Takaichi, the Japanese prime minister.

Then, later this week, Trump will take part in the first trilateral summit between China’s Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Here’s more about what we can expect this week from my colleague Robert Tait:

Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the nail-biting race for US Senate in Alaska.

With 97% of the ballots counted, Peltola – a former congresswoman – has 49.9% of the vote and only needs more than 50% to win.

At present, Sullivan only has 46% of the vote. This would be the Democrats’ ninth flip of the midterms cycle and the first time the party has won a US Senate since 2009.

On Sunday Trump continued to blast Ana Reyes, the federal judge appointed by Joe Biden, who has temporarily blocked construction on the historic Washington public golf course that the president wants to turn it ⁠into a championship-level course.

“Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?” Trump wrote on Truth Social, noting that his administration plans to appeal the ruling. “Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!”

US air travel was slowly returning to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US aviation authorities.

The ground stop issued on Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.

On Monday morning, more than 250 US-related flights – those traveling within, into or out of the United States – scheduled for the same day were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.

That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 2,300 flights cancelled on Sunday.

There were delays to more than 700 US-related flights scheduled for Monday, compared to more than 10,000 the previous day, AFP reported.

A progressive and onetime presidential candidate, Senator Elizabeth Warren is a vocal Wall Street critic and has repeatedly condemned the Trump administration and its policies.

She is the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, and is widely expected to become chair when Democrats ⁠take over Congress, Reuters reported.

The US Department of ⁠Justice on Sunday warned her of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into Donald Trump.

Aaron Reitz’s letter to Warren cited her statements on investigating corporate leaders. “The ​context sends a strong ​smoke signal: you intend to target private ​individuals close to president Trump,” he wrote.

Other Democratic lawmakers who have ​received similar letters include ‌Senators Richard Blumenthal ​and Elissa Slotkin ​as well as Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to lead the House oversight committee.

Political experts and Trump’s opponents have raised concerns about efforts by the Republican president and his administration to target their own critics and political opponents.
